title: Your team's prompt got worse. Who changed it?
summary:
Someone tweaks one line of the prompt your agent runs on. The next run is worse. A week later nobody can say which edit did it, because the prompt lives in a chat, a Notion page, or a file that never saw version control.

Sound familiar? That is the problem I'm building PromptLikeEngineer for (disclosure: it's my project). Here is what it looks like in practice, in three small steps.

1. Find out what changed

Every committed edit becomes a version (right away from the terminal, when you hit Commit on the web). Pick any two and you see exactly what was added and removed, section by section (role, context, instructions). Red is gone, green is new.

Prefer the terminal? Two commands:

ple log pr-review
ple diff pr-review 1 2

2. Undo without losing anything

The new version is worse? Go back:

ple rollback pr-review 1

Here is the part I like: a rollback doesn't delete anything. It saves the old text as a new version, so the bad edit stays in the history and you can still learn from it.

3. Work on it together

On the Team plan, everyone shares one library and has a role (admin, editor or viewer). Anyone can improve a prompt, and every version shows who made it. "Who changed this?" finally has an answer.

Prompts are plain Markdown. You can add {{variables}} and small {{#if}} blocks, so one prompt can cover a few cases instead of living in four copies:

{{#if focus}}Pay extra attention to: {{focus}}{{/if}}

ple get prints a prompt in the terminal, so you can use it from whatever tool you like. There is also a Claude Code plugin (MCP) that lets an agent read and update prompts. I've only tested that part with Claude Code, so I can't promise more.

What it doesn't do

It keeps track of your prompt text. It doesn't run the prompt and it doesn't check whether the output got better. One reader pointed out that the strongest setup keeps a small test example next to the prompt, so every change is tried on a realistic input before it ships. That part is still on you, and I'd love to hear how you handle it.

Want to poke at it?

You can save, compare and roll back a prompt right in your browser, no account needed: promptlikeengineer.com/try. It's early, so tell me what's missing.

title: Liveness vs Readiness Probe: Kubernetes Config That Avoids Restart Loops
summary:
This guide was written by Michael Zion, CEO at MeteorOps, and first published on the MeteorOps blog.

Bottom line

A Kubernetes liveness probe tells the kubelet when to restart a container; a readiness probe only removes the pod from Service traffic and never restarts it. To avoid restart loops, keep liveness checks local to the process, move dependency checks to readiness, use a startupProbe for slow boots, and set timeouts of 2 to 3 seconds.

The goal is not to make liveness probes pass more often. It is to use them only for conditions a restart can actually fix, and to give the application enough time to prove it is truly wedged before Kubernetes kills it.

Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes

Probe Question it answers What happens on failure What it should check
livenessProbe Is the process wedged beyond recovery? The kubelet kills and restarts the container (per restartPolicy). Local process health only: event loop responsive, no fatal internal state.
readinessProbe Can this pod take traffic right now? The pod is removed from Service endpoints. No restart. Dependencies, warm caches, draining state.
startupProbe Has the app finished booting? Liveness and readiness are held back until it passes. If it never passes within failureThreshold x periodSeconds, the container is restarted. Initialization complete: migrations, cache load, model load.


Only liveness and startup failures restart the container; readiness only controls traffic.

Understand what a liveness probe is allowed to do

A liveness probe answers one narrow question: “Should Kubernetes restart this container?” If the probe fails enough times, the kubelet restarts the container according to the pod’s restart policy. That is powerful, but it is also blunt.

A liveness probe should detect problems such as:

  • A process deadlock where the application stops serving all useful work.

  • A stuck event loop that no longer responds locally.

  • A broken internal state that only a process restart can clear.

  • A worker process that is alive at the operating system level but cannot make progress.

A liveness probe should usually avoid checking:

  • Database reachability.

  • Message broker availability.

  • Third-party API status.

  • Availability of another internal service.

  • Long-running migrations or warm-up tasks.

If the database is unavailable and every pod fails its liveness probe because of that database check, Kubernetes will restart every pod. The restart will not fix the database. It will add load, increase cold starts, clear in-memory caches, and make recovery harder.


Put dependency checks in readiness so an outage removes pods from traffic instead of restarting them all.

Use the right probe for the right job:

  • startupProbe: gives slow-starting containers time to initialize before liveness checks begin.

  • readinessProbe: controls whether the pod receives traffic.

  • livenessProbe: restarts the container when it is truly unhealthy.

If you manage Kubernetes manifests through infrastructure as code, keep this distinction explicit in your modules or templates. The same principle applies whether you apply raw YAML, use Helm, or deploy Kubernetes resources using Terraform.

Start with a safe baseline configuration

Begin with conservative thresholds, then tighten them after observing real startup time and failure behavior. Do not copy probe values across services without checking how each service starts, warms up, and handles load.

Here is a risky liveness probe:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/api:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 1
            failureThreshold: 3

This can restart the container after roughly 20 seconds: 5 seconds of initial delay, then 3 failed probes spaced 5 seconds apart. If the service sometimes needs 45 seconds to load configuration, run migrations, compile templates, or warm caches, this pod can restart forever.

A safer pattern separates startup, readiness, and liveness:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/api:1.0.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080

          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /startupz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 24

          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3
            successThreshold: 1

          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /livez
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 3

In this example, the startup probe allows up to about 120 seconds for startup: 24 failures multiplied by a 5-second period. While the startup probe is still failing, Kubernetes does not run the liveness probe. After startup succeeds, liveness begins.


A startupProbe window longer than slow startup lets the app finish booting before liveness can restart it.

This matters for applications with variable boot times, such as Java services, applications that load large models, services that hydrate caches, or workers that recover state during startup.

Use practical threshold math before shipping

You should be able to explain every probe value in a deployment review. If the answer is “we copied it,” the probe is not tuned.

Use this rough calculation:

restart window ≈ initialDelaySeconds + (failureThreshold × periodSeconds)

For a liveness probe like this:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: http
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3

Kubernetes may restart the container after about 60 seconds of failing liveness checks. That may be fine for a stateless API with a 10-second normal startup time. It may be too aggressive for a batch worker that can pause during garbage collection, checkpoint recovery, or CPU pressure.

Use these starting points as a practical baseline, then adjust with real data:

  • startupProbe: set failureThreshold × periodSeconds higher than your slow but acceptable startup time. If p95 startup is 70 seconds, start around 120 seconds.

  • readinessProbe: keep it responsive. A period of 5 to 10 seconds is common because it controls traffic routing.

  • livenessProbe: keep it less aggressive than readiness. A period of 10 to 30 seconds with a failure threshold of 3 is a safer default for many services.

  • timeoutSeconds: avoid the default of 1 second for applications that can pause briefly under load. Start with 2 or 3 seconds if you have no better data.

  • initialDelaySeconds: prefer startupProbe for startup handling. Use initialDelaySeconds only when startup behavior is simple and predictable.

Probe tuning should live next to deployment configuration, not in someone’s notes. If your platform team provisions services and dependencies through Kubernetes-native control planes, document probe defaults in the same place you manage patterns such as deploying AWS resources using Crossplane on Kubernetes.

Design health endpoints that match probe intent

The endpoint behind the probe matters more than the YAML. A clean probe configuration still fails if /health does too much work.

A good pattern is to expose separate endpoints:

  • /livez: checks that the process can respond and has not entered a fatal internal state.

  • /readyz: checks whether the application can serve traffic right now.

  • /startupz: checks whether initialization has completed.

For example, an HTTP service might implement behavior like this:

GET /livez
200 OK if the process event loop is responsive
500 only if the process is internally unrecoverable

GET /readyz
200 OK if the service can accept traffic
503 if required dependencies are unavailable or the app is draining

GET /startupz
200 OK after bootstrapping is complete
503 while migrations, cache loading, or state recovery are still running

Here is a minimal Node.js example that keeps liveness local and pushes dependency checks into readiness:

import express from "express";

const app = express();

let started = false;
let shuttingDown = false;

async function checkDatabase() {
  // Replace with a cheap ping or connection-pool status check.
  // Do not run expensive queries here.
  return true;
}

app.get("/startupz", (req, res) => {
  if (started) {
    return res.status(200).send("ok");
  }

  return res.status(503).send("starting");
});

app.get("/livez", (req, res) => {
  // Keep this local. Do not check the database, cache, or third-party APIs.
  return res.status(200).send("ok");
});

app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
  if (shuttingDown || !started) {
    return res.status(503).send("not ready");
  }

  const databaseOk = await checkDatabase();

  if (!databaseOk) {
    return res.status(503).send("database unavailable");
  }

  return res.status(200).send("ok");
});

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  shuttingDown = true;
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 10_000);
});

app.listen(8080, async () => {
  // Run startup work here.
  started = true;
});

For worker services without HTTP servers, an exec probe can work, but use it carefully. Every probe spawns a process inside the container. At scale, expensive exec probes can add measurable overhead.

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - test -f /tmp/worker-alive
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 4

If you use an exec probe, keep the command fast and deterministic. Avoid commands that call external systems, perform file tree scans, invoke package managers, or depend on shells that may not exist in minimal images.

Roll out probe changes with evidence

Treat probe changes like production behavior changes. They can cause restarts, remove pods from service, and change rollout timing.

Use this rollout process:

  1. Measure current startup time. Check container logs, application metrics, and Kubernetes events. Record typical and slow startup durations.

  2. Add or tune startupProbe. Make sure the allowed startup window exceeds slow but valid startup.

  3. Split liveness and readiness endpoints. Keep restart logic separate from traffic-routing logic.

  4. Deploy to a small scope first. Use one environment, one namespace, or one replica set before changing every workload.

  5. Watch events during rollout. Confirm that restarts are not increasing unexpectedly.

  6. Load test or replay traffic if possible. Validate that probes still pass during CPU pressure, garbage collection pauses, and dependency latency.

Useful commands:

kubectl get pods -n app

kubectl describe pod -n app api-7c9f6d8f7f-x2abc

kubectl logs -n app api-7c9f6d8f7f-x2abc --previous

kubectl get events -n app --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Look for messages like:

Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
Back-off restarting failed container
Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.0.1.25:8080/readyz": context deadline exceeded

If --previous logs show that the application was still starting when it was killed, your startup window is too short or your liveness probe is starting too early. If logs show request latency spikes before liveness failures, your timeout may be too low or the endpoint may share overloaded application threads.

When Kubernetes is part of a larger platform rollout, probe settings should be reviewed with resource requests, limits, rollout strategy, and dependency provisioning. For example, an application deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) can still fail because a probe ignores slow boot behavior, even if the cluster itself is healthy. The same operational checks apply when you deploy Apache Airflow on AWS EKS or run a custom API service.

Avoid the common liveness probe traps

Most restart loops come from a few repeatable mistakes.

Trap 1: Dependency checks in liveness

If /livez fails when PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, or an external API is unavailable, you are asking Kubernetes to restart your application because another system has a problem.

Move dependency checks to readiness:

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: http
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: http
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 4

Trap 2: No startup probe for slow applications

initialDelaySeconds can work for simple services, but it is a fixed delay. It does not adapt to real startup progress. A startupProbe lets Kubernetes wait until startup succeeds, then begins liveness checks.

Use startup probes for services with:

  • Large dependency injection graphs.

  • Database migrations or schema checks.

  • Cache warm-up.

  • Model loading.

  • State recovery after shutdown.

Trap 3: Timeout too low under CPU pressure

The default timeoutSeconds is 1 second. That can be too low for applications under CPU throttling, garbage collection, or temporary I/O pressure.

If probes fail during load but the application recovers without a restart, increase timeoutSeconds, increase failureThreshold, or make the probe endpoint cheaper. Also check CPU limits. A pod with a tight CPU limit can fail probes because the process cannot get scheduled quickly enough.

Trap 4: Redirects, auth, or middleware on health routes

Health endpoints should avoid authentication middleware, redirects, rate limits, and expensive request logging. The kubelet counts any status from 200 to 399 as success, so 401, 403 and 5xx responses fail the probe. Redirects to the same host are followed; a redirect to a different host is treated as success with a warning event, which can hide a broken endpoint.

Make health routes boring:

  • Return directly from the application.

  • Do not require tokens.

  • Do not redirect HTTP to HTTPS inside the pod unless the probe is configured for HTTPS.

  • Do not call external services from liveness.

Trap 5: Probe port does not match the container

Named ports reduce mistakes when container ports change:

ports:
  - name: http
    containerPort: 8080

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: http

If you use service meshes or sidecars, confirm whether the kubelet probes the application container directly or whether probe rewriting is active. Misconfigured sidecar behavior can make a healthy application look unhealthy.

Fix the common probe error messages

These are the exact strings you will see in kubectl describe pod and kubectl get events, with what they usually mean.


Each common probe error points to a different fix, so read the event message before changing thresholds.

Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500

The endpoint answered, but with an error. Usually /livez runs dependency checks (database, cache, another service) that are down. Make liveness local and move those checks to readiness. If the app really returns 500 because it is broken, check kubectl logs POD --previous for the cause of the crash before tuning anything.

Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.0.1.25:8080/livez": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)

The endpoint did not answer within timeoutSeconds (default 1 second). Common causes are CPU throttling from a tight CPU limit, garbage collection pauses, or the health route sharing a saturated thread pool. Raise timeoutSeconds to 2 or 3, raise failureThreshold, and check CPU throttling metrics.

Liveness probe failed: dial tcp 10.0.1.25:8080: connect: connection refused

Nothing is listening yet, or the probe points at the wrong port. During startup this means the liveness probe started too early: add a startupProbe. Otherwise, check that the probe port matches the container port, ideally by using a named port.

Back-off restarting failed container

The container restarted several times and the kubelet is now waiting with an exponential back-off (up to 5 minutes) before the next attempt. The pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Find whether the restarts come from probe failures (events say "Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted") or from the process exiting on its own (exit code in kubectl describe pod).

Readiness probe failed but the container is not restarting

That is expected. Readiness failures only remove the pod from Service endpoints. If the pod never becomes ready, fix the dependency or the readiness logic; restarts will not help.

Use this final checklist before merging

Before you merge a liveness probe change, verify these points:

  • /livez checks only local process health.

  • /readyz handles dependency checks and traffic eligibility.

  • /startupz exists for slow or variable startup.

  • The startup window is longer than slow but valid startup time.

  • The liveness restart window is long enough to survive short pauses.

  • timeoutSeconds is realistic for your runtime and CPU limits.

  • Health endpoints bypass auth, redirects, and expensive middleware.

  • Probe failures are visible in logs, metrics, or Kubernetes events.

  • The rollout plan limits blast radius.

FAQ

Does a readiness probe failure restart the container?

No. Only liveness and startup probe failures restart a container. A failing readiness probe removes the pod from Service endpoints until it passes again.

Does a startup probe failure restart the container?

Yes. If the startup probe keeps failing past failureThreshold x periodSeconds, the kubelet kills the container and restarts it, just like a liveness failure.

What are good default liveness probe values?

A practical starting point is periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 2 and failureThreshold: 3, with a startupProbe covering your slowest normal boot. Tune from observed startup time and pause behavior, not copied defaults. The official reference is the Kubernetes guide to configuring liveness, readiness and startup probes.

Should a liveness probe check the database?

No. If the database goes down, every pod fails liveness and restarts at once, which adds load and slows recovery without fixing anything. Check dependencies in readiness.

Can I use the same endpoint for liveness and readiness?

You can, but it is a common source of restart loops. Separate /livez and /readyz endpoints let readiness react to dependencies while liveness stays local.

Liveness probes are useful when they restart containers that cannot recover on their own. They become dangerous when they replace readiness checks, dependency monitoring, or startup handling. Start conservative, separate probe responsibilities, watch real failure events, and tune based on observed behavior rather than copied defaults.

  return res.status(503).send("starting");
});

app.get("/livez", (req, res) => {
  // Keep this local. Do not check the database, cache, or third-party APIs.
  return res.status(200).send("ok");
});

app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
  if (shuttingDown || !started) {
    return res.status(503).send("not ready");
  }

  const databaseOk = await checkDatabase();

  if (!databaseOk) {
    return res.status(503).send("database unavailable");
  }

  return res.status(200).send("ok");
});

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  shuttingDown = true;
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 10_000);
});

  // Run startup work here.
  started = true;
});

For worker services without HTTP servers, an exec probe can work, but use it carefully. Every probe spawns a process inside the container. At scale, expensive exec probes can add measurable overhead.

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - test -f /tmp/worker-alive
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 4

If you use an exec probe, keep the command fast and deterministic. Avoid commands that call external systems, perform file tree scans, invoke package managers, or depend on shells that may not exist in minimal images.

Roll out probe changes with evidence

Treat probe changes like production behavior changes. They can cause restarts, remove pods from service, and change rollout timing.

Use this rollout process:

  1. Measure current startup time. Check container logs, application metrics, and Kubernetes events. Record typical and slow startup durations.

  2. Add or tune startupProbe. Make sure the allowed startup window exceeds slow but valid startup.

  3. Split liveness and readiness endpoints. Keep restart logic separate from traffic-routing logic.

  4. Deploy to a small scope first. Use one environment, one namespace, or one replica set before changing every workload.

  5. Watch events during rollout. Confirm that restarts are not increasing unexpectedly.

  6. Load test or replay traffic if possible. Validate that probes still pass during CPU pressure, garbage collection pauses, and dependency latency.

Useful commands:

kubectl get pods -n app

kubectl describe pod -n app api-7c9f6d8f7f-x2abc

kubectl logs -n app api-7c9f6d8f7f-x2abc --previous

kubectl get events -n app --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Look for messages like:

Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
Back-off restarting failed container
Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.0.1.25:8080/readyz": context deadline exceeded

If --previous logs show that the application was still starting when it was killed, your startup window is too short or your liveness probe is starting too early. If logs show request latency spikes before liveness failures, your timeout may be too low or the endpoint may share overloaded application threads.

When Kubernetes is part of a larger platform rollout, probe settings should be reviewed with resource requests, limits, rollout strategy, and dependency provisioning. For example, an application deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) can still fail because a probe ignores slow boot behavior, even if the cluster itself is healthy. The same operational checks apply when you deploy Apache Airflow on AWS EKS or run a custom API service.

Avoid the common liveness probe traps

Most restart loops come from a few repeatable mistakes.

Trap 1: Dependency checks in liveness

If /livez fails when PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, or an external API is unavailable, you are asking Kubernetes to restart your application because another system has a problem.

Move dependency checks to readiness:

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: http
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: http
  periodSeconds: 15
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 4

Trap 2: No startup probe for slow applications

initialDelaySeconds can work for simple services, but it is a fixed delay. It does not adapt to real startup progress. A startupProbe lets Kubernetes wait until startup succeeds, then begins liveness checks.

Use startup probes for services with:

  • Large dependency injection graphs.

  • Database migrations or schema checks.

  • Cache warm-up.

  • Model loading.

  • State recovery after shutdown.

Trap 3: Timeout too low under CPU pressure

The default timeoutSeconds is 1 second. That can be too low for applications under CPU throttling, garbage collection, or temporary I/O pressure.

If probes fail during load but the application recovers without a restart, increase timeoutSeconds, increase failureThreshold, or make the probe endpoint cheaper. Also check CPU limits. A pod with a tight CPU limit can fail probes because the process cannot get scheduled quickly enough.

Trap 4: Redirects, auth, or middleware on health routes

Health endpoints should avoid authentication middleware, redirects, rate limits, and expensive request logging. The kubelet counts any status from 200 to 399 as success, so 401, 403 and 5xx responses fail the probe. Redirects to the same host are followed; a redirect to a different host is treated as success with a warning event, which can hide a broken endpoint.

Make health routes boring:

  • Return directly from the application.

  • Do not require tokens.

  • Do not redirect HTTP to HTTPS inside the pod unless the probe is configured for HTTPS.

  • Do not call external services from liveness.

Trap 5: Probe port does not match the container

Named ports reduce mistakes when container ports change:

ports:
  - name: http
    containerPort: 8080

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /livez
    port: http

If you use service meshes or sidecars, confirm whether the kubelet probes the application container directly or whether probe rewriting is active. Misconfigured sidecar behavior can make a healthy application look unhealthy.

Fix the common probe error messages

These are the exact strings you will see in kubectl describe pod and kubectl get events, with what they usually mean.


Each common probe error points to a different fix, so read the event message before changing thresholds.

Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500

The endpoint answered, but with an error. Usually /livez runs dependency checks (database, cache, another service) that are down. Make liveness local and move those checks to readiness. If the app really returns 500 because it is broken, check kubectl logs POD --previous for the cause of the crash before tuning anything.

Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.0.1.25:8080/livez": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)

The endpoint did not answer within timeoutSeconds (default 1 second). Common causes are CPU throttling from a tight CPU limit, garbage collection pauses, or the health route sharing a saturated thread pool. Raise timeoutSeconds to 2 or 3, raise failureThreshold, and check CPU throttling metrics.

Liveness probe failed: dial tcp 10.0.1.25:8080: connect: connection refused

Nothing is listening yet, or the probe points at the wrong port. During startup this means the liveness probe started too early: add a startupProbe. Otherwise, check that the probe port matches the container port, ideally by using a named port.

Back-off restarting failed container

The container restarted several times and the kubelet is now waiting with an exponential back-off (up to 5 minutes) before the next attempt. The pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Find whether the restarts come from probe failures (events say "Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted") or from the process exiting on its own (exit code in kubectl describe pod).

Readiness probe failed but the container is not restarting

That is expected. Readiness failures only remove the pod from Service endpoints. If the pod never becomes ready, fix the dependency or the readiness logic; restarts will not help.

Use this final checklist before merging

Before you merge a liveness probe change, verify these points:

  • /livez checks only local process health.

  • /readyz handles dependency checks and traffic eligibility.

  • /startupz exists for slow or variable startup.

  • The startup window is longer than slow but valid startup time.

  • The liveness restart window is long enough to survive short pauses.

  • timeoutSeconds is realistic for your runtime and CPU limits.

  • Health endpoints bypass auth, redirects, and expensive middleware.

  • Probe failures are visible in logs, metrics, or Kubernetes events.

  • The rollout plan limits blast radius.

FAQ

Does a readiness probe failure restart the container?

No. Only liveness and startup probe failures restart a container. A failing readiness probe removes the pod from Service endpoints until it passes again.

Does a startup probe failure restart the container?

Yes. If the startup probe keeps failing past failureThreshold x periodSeconds, the kubelet kills the container and restarts it, just like a liveness failure.

What are good default liveness probe values?

A practical starting point is periodSeconds: 10, timeoutSeconds: 2 and failureThreshold: 3, with a startupProbe covering your slowest normal boot. Tune from observed startup time and pause behavior, not copied defaults. The official reference is the Kubernetes guide to configuring liveness, readiness and startup probes.

Should a liveness probe check the database?

No. If the database goes down, every pod fails liveness and restarts at once, which adds load and slows recovery without fixing anything. Check dependencies in readiness.

Can I use the same endpoint for liveness and readiness?

You can, but it is a common source of restart loops. Separate /livez and /readyz endpoints let readiness react to dependencies while liveness stays local.

Liveness probes are useful when they restart containers that cannot recover on their own. They become dangerous when they replace readiness checks, dependency monitoring, or startup handling. Start conservative, separate probe responsibilities, watch real failure events, and tune based on observed behavior rather than copied defaults.

title: Actively exploited this week: 3 new CISA KEV entries (2 November to 8 November 2026)
summary:
Every week CISA adds vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The bar for getting on that list is not "severe on paper" but "attackers are using it now". For a small team with limited patching hours, that makes KEV the most useful priority list there is.

Below: every entry added between 2 November and 8 November 2026, copied from the catalogue and linked to its NVD record, plus what Romania's national cyber security directorate and Have I Been Pwned published in the same days. Nothing is estimated or rewritten.

The 3 actively exploited vulnerabilities added this week

Added Product CVE Known ransomware use
6 Nov SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-19868 not known
4 Nov Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2024-27834 not known
3 Nov WordPress WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability CVE-2026-119977 not known

What Romania's DNSC flagged the same week

Alerts from DNSC, Romania's national cyber security directorate, with their original titles in Romanian:

  • ALERTĂ: Vulnerabilități critice exploatate activ în Synology, 6 November

When a national authority and CISA point at the same product in the same week, that product goes to the top of the queue.

Breaches added to Have I Been Pwned

  • Harvard: 850,537 accounts, added 3 November. Check the breach page

If your team's work addresses may be in one of these, check the breach page and the password reuse question, not only the address.

How to use a list like this in an hour

  1. Start with what faces the internet. VPN and access gateways, firewalls, routers, mail servers and public web platforms are how many ransomware incidents start.
  2. Search your inventory by product name, not by memory. "We don't run that" is a claim, and the asset list is the evidence.
  3. Patch or apply the vendor mitigation, then confirm the version. A patch that was downloaded but not applied reads as done in a ticket and is still exploitable.
  4. If you cannot patch today, reduce exposure: restrict the management interface to known addresses, disable the affected feature, or put the service behind an access gateway you trust.

Where this comes from

A small collector reads official sources every hour: DNSC, CERT-EU, CERT-FR (ANSSI), CERT-Bund (BSI), the UK NCSC, CISA KEV, Have I Been Pwned and three specialist newsrooms. It copies each item exactly, with its source link, and publishes the result on one page:

https://devaland.cloud/alerte-live.html (in Romanian, with every title kept in its original language).

Nothing on that page or in this post is written by a model. A security page that paraphrases an advisory wrongly does more harm than no page at all.

title: Why Log Redaction Alone Won't Save Your API Keys
summary:
API keys are the quietest breach vector in most codebases. They sit in environment variables, config files, and request headers — and every time your application logs a request for debugging, there is a chance one of them lands in plaintext in a log aggregator. Redaction tools promise to clean that up. In practice, they are the last line of defense, not the first.

Why redaction fails

Redaction at the log ingestion layer works by pattern matching. It looks for strings that resemble known secret formats — sk_live_..., AWS key shapes, UUIDs — and replaces them with a placeholder. That works until it doesn't.

  • Regex is structure, not intent. A key split across a JSON boundary, base64-encoded, or embedded in a nested payload can slip past a pattern that expects a contiguous string.
  • Formats change. Internal gateways, third-party SDKs, and homegrown auth schemes all produce credentials that do not match the vendor's list.
  • Pressure weakens the filter. During a production incident, teams routinely raise log verbosity and relax redaction rules to see more. That is exactly when a key gets logged.

The better default: do not log the secret

The most reliable redaction is the one you never need. Treat logging as a data-minimization problem:

  1. Log a derived identifier, not the secret. Store a key ID or the last four characters alongside the secret in your vault. Log the identifier.
  2. Fetch secrets at runtime, never at boot. Use a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) and short-lived credentials. The application authenticates to the vault with its own identity, reads the secret, uses it, and never passes the raw value through a log statement.
  3. Redact at the source, not the sink. Add a logging serializer that strips Authorization, Cookie, api_key, and similar fields before the record is written.

Test the pipeline, not just the pattern

A redaction rule that works in a unit test can fail in production. Prove it end to end:

  • Fuzz the logging middleware with known secrets in JSON, query strings, headers, and error stack traces.
  • Trace a request from the ingress gateway through the service and logging library to the final sink, and assert that the secret never appears in any of them.
  • Add an automated check that fails the build if a known test key shows up in captured logs. 
import re

def assert_no_secret(log_entry: str, pattern: str) -> None:
    if re.search(pattern, log_entry):
        raise AssertionError("sensitive pattern found in log")

Rotate like a key is already leaked

Assume every long-lived key will eventually be exposed. Automate rotation on a schedule — 90 days for most keys, 30 for database and payment credentials — and use a grace period where old and new keys both work so rotation does not cause an outage.

The goal is not a perfect regex. It is a design where a missed redaction cannot turn into a breach.

This is an expanded technical note based on our analysis. The original is here: https://hsecurities.in/blog/api-key-survives-log-redaction

title: Load Balancer Internals: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB, and What Actually Happens to a Packet
summary:
The question "ALB or NLB?" usually gets answered by feature comparison — ALB has path-based routing, NLB has static IPs. That's not wrong, but it skips the decision that actually matters first: which OSI layer does your traffic need to be load balanced at. ALB operates at Layer 7, NLB at Layer 4, and GWLB at Layer 3, and that single distinction determines far more about behavior, performance, and what's even possible than any feature checklist does.

This article works through each type by what it actually does to a packet — connection handling, health check granularity, cross-zone cost model, and the failure modes each type produces in production.

ALB: Layer 7 — terminates the connection

ALB terminates the client's TCP connection entirely, reads the actual HTTP request — method, path, headers, host — and makes a routing decision based on that content before opening a new, separate TCP connection to the chosen backend.

Client ──TCP/TLS──> ALB ──reads HTTP request──> routing decision
                      │
                      └──new TCP connection──> Target (backend)

This connection termination is the architectural fact that explains everything else ALB can do. Because it's parsing HTTP, it can route on path (/api/* to one target group, /static/* to another), host header, or query parameters — none of which are visible to a load balancer that only sees TCP segments.

resource "aws_lb_listener_rule" "api_route" {
  listener_arn = aws_lb_listener.https.arn
  priority     = 100

  action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.api.arn
  }

  condition {
    path_pattern {
      values = ["/api/*"]
    }
  }
}

The cost: ALB adds processing latency per request, and because it terminates TLS, the backend sees the ALB's IP as the source — not the client's real IP — unless you read it from the X-Forwarded-For header ALB injects. This is a frequent source of confusion in application logs and IP-based rate limiting logic that wasn't written with a Layer 7 proxy in mind.

NLB: Layer 4 — preserves the connection

NLB doesn't terminate the client connection or read anything above the transport layer. It forwards packets to a chosen target based on a consistent hash of the connection's 5-tuple, and the TCP connection stays intact end-to-end between client and target.

Client ──TCP connection (same connection throughout)──> NLB ──> Target
                                                            (NLB forwards, doesn't terminate)

Two direct consequences: the backend sees the client's actual source IP by default — no X-Forwarded-For needed — and NLB can sustain millions of requests per second with single-digit-millisecond latency, because it isn't doing HTTP parsing or connection re-establishment.

resource "aws_lb" "network" {
  name               = "nlb-tcp-service"
  load_balancer_type = "network"
  subnets            = [aws_subnet.public_a.id, aws_subnet.public_b.id]

  enable_cross_zone_load_balancing = true
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "tcp" {
  name        = "tg-tcp-service"
  port        = 5432
  protocol    = "TCP"
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.main.id
  target_type = "ip"

  health_check {
    protocol = "TCP"
    port     = "5432"
  }
}

NLB also supports assigning a static Elastic IP per Availability Zone — something ALB architecturally cannot do. This is the single most common reason teams choose NLB even for HTTP traffic: the static IP requirement alone rules out ALB regardless of everything else.

GWLB: Layer 3 — transparent network insertion

GWLB solves a genuinely different problem: inserting third-party network appliances — firewalls, IDS/IPS, deep packet inspection tools — transparently into a traffic path, without the appliance needing to be the traffic's actual destination.

Client traffic ──> GWLB ──> Appliance (inspects/filters) ──> GWLB ──> original destination
                     (via GENEVE encapsulation, traffic returns through GWLB)

GWLB uses GENEVE encapsulation (port 6081) to wrap the original traffic and send it to a fleet of appliance instances, which inspect or transform it and send it back through the same GWLB endpoint. ALB and NLB sit in the traffic path as the thing clients connect to; GWLB sits beside the traffic path, transparently redirecting traffic through an appliance fleet without the client or destination needing any awareness.

resource "aws_lb" "gateway" {
  name               = "gwlb-firewall-fleet"
  load_balancer_type = "gateway"
  subnets            = [aws_subnet.appliance_a.id, aws_subnet.appliance_b.id]
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "gwlb" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name       = aws_vpc_endpoint_service.gwlb.service_name
  vpc_endpoint_type  = "GatewayLoadBalancer"
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.private_a.id]
}

Most teams never need GWLB directly unless they're deploying a specific third-party security appliance that integrates with it, or building a centralized inspection architecture across many VPCs in an AWS Organization.

Health checks: where the layer difference matters most

ALB health checks are HTTP/HTTPS requests expecting a specific status code range — a target returning 500 consistently is marked unhealthy even if the TCP port is accepting connections fine. NLB's default health check is often just a TCP connection check, which only confirms the port is accepting connections, not that the application is functioning correctly. A target that accepts TCP connections but can't process the specific protocol correctly passes NLB health checks while still failing real requests.

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "api" {
  name     = "tg-api"
  port     = 443
  protocol = "HTTPS"
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id

  health_check {
    path                = "/health"
    matcher             = "200"
    interval            = 15
    healthy_threshold   = 2
    unhealthy_threshold = 3
    timeout             = 5
  }
}

The asymmetric thresholds (2 to become healthy, 3 to become unhealthy) are deliberate — the cost of routing to a still-recovering target is usually higher than slightly slower failure detection.

Cross-zone load balancing: a cost detail that differs by type

For ALB, cross-zone load balancing is enabled by default and free. For NLB, it is disabled by default, and enabling it incurs standard cross-AZ data transfer charges for any request forwarded to a target in a different AZ. This is worth being deliberate about specifically because NLB is often chosen for high-throughput workloads — exactly the situation where an unexpected cross-AZ data transfer bill shows up fastest.

Side-by-side summary

ALB NLB GWLB
OSI layer 7 (Application) 4 (Transport) 3 (Network)
Connection handling Terminates and re-establishes Forwards, preserves end-to-end Transparent redirect via GENEVE
Protocols HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket TCP, UDP, TLS passthrough Any IP traffic
Client source IP visible to backend Via X-Forwarded-For only Natively, by default N/A
Static IP support No Yes, per AZ N/A
Content-based routing Yes (path, host, headers) No No

  • The four most common production failure modes for each type (ALB 502s, NLB health check blind spots, GWLB return routing, missing source IP after switching types)
  • The "topic fan-out into per-consumer queues" pattern and when to reach for a log instead
  • Why "exactly-once" delivery guarantees are narrower than the name suggests across SQS FIFO, Service Bus, and Kafka transactions

  condition {
    path_pattern {
      values = ["/api/*"]
    }
  }
}

The cost: ALB adds processing latency per request, and because it terminates TLS, the backend sees the ALB's IP as the source — not the client's real IP — unless you read it from the X-Forwarded-For header ALB injects. This is a frequent source of confusion in application logs and IP-based rate limiting logic that wasn't written with a Layer 7 proxy in mind.

NLB: Layer 4 — preserves the connection

NLB doesn't terminate the client connection or read anything above the transport layer. It forwards packets to a chosen target based on a consistent hash of the connection's 5-tuple, and the TCP connection stays intact end-to-end between client and target.

Client ──TCP connection (same connection throughout)──> NLB ──> Target
                                                            (NLB forwards, doesn't terminate)

Two direct consequences: the backend sees the client's actual source IP by default — no X-Forwarded-For needed — and NLB can sustain millions of requests per second with single-digit-millisecond latency, because it isn't doing HTTP parsing or connection re-establishment.

resource "aws_lb" "network" {
  name               = "nlb-tcp-service"
  load_balancer_type = "network"
  subnets            = [aws_subnet.public_a.id, aws_subnet.public_b.id]

  enable_cross_zone_load_balancing = true
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "tcp" {
  name        = "tg-tcp-service"
  port        = 5432
  protocol    = "TCP"
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.main.id
  target_type = "ip"

  health_check {
    protocol = "TCP"
    port     = "5432"
  }
}

NLB also supports assigning a static Elastic IP per Availability Zone — something ALB architecturally cannot do. This is the single most common reason teams choose NLB even for HTTP traffic: the static IP requirement alone rules out ALB regardless of everything else.

GWLB: Layer 3 — transparent network insertion

GWLB solves a genuinely different problem: inserting third-party network appliances — firewalls, IDS/IPS, deep packet inspection tools — transparently into a traffic path, without the appliance needing to be the traffic's actual destination.

Client traffic ──> GWLB ──> Appliance (inspects/filters) ──> GWLB ──> original destination
                     (via GENEVE encapsulation, traffic returns through GWLB)

GWLB uses GENEVE encapsulation (port 6081) to wrap the original traffic and send it to a fleet of appliance instances, which inspect or transform it and send it back through the same GWLB endpoint. ALB and NLB sit in the traffic path as the thing clients connect to; GWLB sits beside the traffic path, transparently redirecting traffic through an appliance fleet without the client or destination needing any awareness.

resource "aws_lb" "gateway" {
  name               = "gwlb-firewall-fleet"
  load_balancer_type = "gateway"
  subnets            = [aws_subnet.appliance_a.id, aws_subnet.appliance_b.id]
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "gwlb" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name       = aws_vpc_endpoint_service.gwlb.service_name
  vpc_endpoint_type  = "GatewayLoadBalancer"
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.private_a.id]
}

Most teams never need GWLB directly unless they're deploying a specific third-party security appliance that integrates with it, or building a centralized inspection architecture across many VPCs in an AWS Organization.

Health checks: where the layer difference matters most

ALB health checks are HTTP/HTTPS requests expecting a specific status code range — a target returning 500 consistently is marked unhealthy even if the TCP port is accepting connections fine. NLB's default health check is often just a TCP connection check, which only confirms the port is accepting connections, not that the application is functioning correctly. A target that accepts TCP connections but can't process the specific protocol correctly passes NLB health checks while still failing real requests.

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "api" {
  name     = "tg-api"
  port     = 443
  protocol = "HTTPS"
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id

  health_check {
    path                = "/health"
    matcher             = "200"
    interval            = 15
    healthy_threshold   = 2
    unhealthy_threshold = 3
    timeout             = 5
  }
}

The asymmetric thresholds (2 to become healthy, 3 to become unhealthy) are deliberate — the cost of routing to a still-recovering target is usually higher than slightly slower failure detection.

Cross-zone load balancing: a cost detail that differs by type

For ALB, cross-zone load balancing is enabled by default and free. For NLB, it is disabled by default, and enabling it incurs standard cross-AZ data transfer charges for any request forwarded to a target in a different AZ. This is worth being deliberate about specifically because NLB is often chosen for high-throughput workloads — exactly the situation where an unexpected cross-AZ data transfer bill shows up fastest.

Side-by-side summary

ALB NLB GWLB
OSI layer 7 (Application) 4 (Transport) 3 (Network)
Connection handling Terminates and re-establishes Forwards, preserves end-to-end Transparent redirect via GENEVE
Protocols HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket TCP, UDP, TLS passthrough Any IP traffic
Client source IP visible to backend Via X-Forwarded-For only Natively, by default N/A
Static IP support No Yes, per AZ N/A
Content-based routing Yes (path, host, headers) No No

title: 7 Terminal Commands That Make Me Look Like a Wizard (But Are Actually Basic)
summary:
Every team has that one person. You know the one. They type eight characters, hit enter, and suddenly the port conflict is fixed, the file is found, and the server is running — all while you were still reading the error message.

Here's the secret: they're not wizards. They just know a handful of commands that solve the problems you hit every single day. I've collected seven of them. None require installing anything. All of them will make a junior dev watching your screen quietly assume you have root access to the universe.

(Windows folks: everything here works in WSL or Git Bash.)

1. Ctrl+R — search your command history

You ran a long, clever command two weeks ago. It's gone from your memory but not from your shell.

Press Ctrl+R and start typing any part of it — docker, ssh, that weird find invocation — and your shell will find it as you type. Press Enter to run it, or the right arrow to edit it first.

Technically a shortcut, not a command, but it's the single highest-value thing on this list. I use it roughly 40 times a day.

2. sudo !! — rerun the last command, but properly 

$ cat /var/log/syslog
Permission denied
$ sudo !!

!! expands to the previous command. So sudo !! means "run that again, but with the permissions I clearly needed the first time."

The two seconds of smugness this buys you is worth more than the entire article.

3. cd - — jump back to the previous directory

You cd'd into a deeply nested folder, and now you need the one you just came from. Don't retype the path. Don't cd ../...

$ cd -

It's the terminal's "back" button. Pair it with cd (no arguments, jumps home) and you can navigate for a whole day without typing a full path.

4. lsof -i :3000 — find out who's squatting on your port

The classic: EADDRINUSE: address already in use :3000. Something is already running on your port. Something you started 40 minutes ago and forgot.

$ lsof -i :3000
COMMAND   PID  USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
node    41293  you   23u  IPv4  ...      TCP *:3000 (LISTEN)
$ kill -9 41293

Find the PID, kill it, restart your server. This one command has probably saved me more cumulative time than any other on this list. It's the difference between "why won't it start" for 15 minutes and 10 seconds of smug typing.

5. tree -L 2 — see the shape of a project

New repo, 47 directories, no idea where anything lives.

$ tree -L 2

Two levels of the whole project structure, in one screen. Bump it to -L 3 when you need more depth. (It's often not installed by default — brew install tree or apt install tree, one time, done.)

6. watch -n 2 — a command that refreshes itself

Waiting for a file to appear, a build to finish, a GPU to free up? Instead of re-running the command manually every few seconds:

$ watch -n 2 ls -la dist/

It re-runs ls every 2 seconds, in place, and highlights what changed. You just watch. It's a poor man's dashboard and it's glorious.

7. tee — see the output AND keep it

You run a command, it prints 200 lines of something important, and it's gone. You needed that in a file.

$ ./build.sh 2>&1 | tee build.log

tee passes the output to your screen and writes it to build.log at the same time. No more "wait, run that again and pipe it somewhere" — the somewhere is built in.

The real trick

Notice what all seven have in common: none of them are impressive in isolation. They're all things you could do "the long way" in a minute or two.

That's exactly why they read as wizardry. When someone sees you type sudo !! and the problem evaporates, they don't see the 200 times you did it manually before. They just see the fix.

Learn one of these per week. In two months you'll be the person on the team that juniors watch suspiciously.

title: Webhooks That Stopped Arriving: Gap Detection & Reconciliation
summary:
A customer emails: "I cancelled my plan three weeks ago, why was I charged again?" You check the billing provider. The cancellation is there. You check your database. The subscription is still active. Your webhook handler has no errors, because for three weeks it received nothing to fail on. The provider disabled your endpoint after a run of failed deliveries, sent one email to an address nobody reads, and moved on.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every migration, query and command myself. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and at Loop Origin we build and maintain SaaS backends that depend on payment, shipping and identity webhooks. This is Part 2 of the series Silent Failures in Production SaaS. Part 1 covered cron jobs that never ran; webhooks are the same class of problem pointed the other way. Your code is fine. The input just stopped.

📚 Series Roadmap — Silent Failures in Production SaaS

  • Part 1: Cron Jobs That Never Ran: Heartbeats & Dead-Man Switches for SaaS
  • Part 2 (This Post): Webhooks That Stopped Arriving: Gap Detection & Reconciliation
  • Part 3: Email That Never Landed: SPF/DKIM/DMARC Drift & Bounce Pipelines
  • Part 4: Config & Feature Flags That Quietly Diverged Across Environments
  • Part 5: Backups That Never Restored: Automated Restore Drills
  • Part 6: Synthetic Checks & SLOs for the Paths Nobody Clicks

Related earlier posts: Webhook Security in Production: HMAC-SHA256 Signatures & Replay Protection · Idempotent Jobs & Exactly-Once Effects · Dead Letter Queues, Poison Messages & Safe Replay Playbooks

How do you detect webhooks that stopped arriving?

Direct answer: Record every received event with its provider event ID, then alert when the receive rate for a source drops below its normal baseline for that time window. Because webhooks are not guaranteed, also run a scheduled reconciliation job that lists recent events or object states from the provider's API and processes anything you missed.

Why webhook gaps are invisible

A webhook integration fails silently in more ways than it fails loudly:

  • Endpoint disabled by the provider. Many providers retry for hours or days, then stop or disable the endpoint after repeated failures. Some, such as GitHub, do not retry automatically at all.
  • Signing secret rotated on one side only. Every request now returns 400 from your signature check, which you may log at debug level.
  • WAF or bot protection starts challenging the provider's IPs after a rule update.
  • Route or domain moved during a refactor, and the provider still posts to the old URL, which now returns a 404 from a catch-all page.
  • New event types were never subscribed, so the feature built on them never receives anything.
  • Received but not processed. The controller stored the payload and queued a job, but the queue worker is down.

None of these throw an exception inside your application. Your error tracker stays green.

Step 1: store every receipt first

Treat the webhook endpoint as an inbox. Verify the signature, store the raw event with a unique constraint, return 2xx fast, and process asynchronously. This gives you the data you need to detect gaps.

// database/migrations/2026_11_09_000000_create_webhook_receipts_table.php
Schema::create('webhook_receipts', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->string('provider', 32);            // stripe, shopify, github...
    $table->string('event_id', 128);
    $table->string('event_type', 128);
    $table->timestampTz('provider_created_at')->nullable();
    $table->timestampTz('received_at')->useCurrent();
    $table->timestampTz('processed_at')->nullable();
    $table->string('source', 16)->default('push');  // push | reconcile
    $table->jsonb('payload');
    $table->unique(['provider', 'event_id']);
    $table->index(['provider', 'received_at']);
});

// app/Http/Controllers/StripeWebhookController.php
public function __invoke(Request $request)
{
    try {
        $event = \Stripe\Webhook::constructEvent(
            $request->getContent(),
            $request->header('Stripe-Signature'),
            config('services.stripe.webhook_secret'),
        );
    } catch (\Throwable $e) {
        // Signature failures must be visible: a rotated secret looks exactly like this.
        Log::warning('stripe_webhook_rejected', ['reason' => $e->getMessage()]);
        return response('invalid', 400);
    }

    $inserted = DB::table('webhook_receipts')->insertOrIgnore([
        'provider' => 'stripe',
        'event_id' => $event->id,
        'event_type' => $event->type,
        'provider_created_at' => Carbon::createFromTimestamp($event->created),
        'payload' => json_encode($event->toArray()),
    ]);

    if ($inserted) {
        ProcessWebhookReceipt::dispatch('stripe', $event->id);
    }

    return response()->noContent();
}

The unique index makes duplicate deliveries and reconciliation overlaps harmless. That idempotency is what lets you reconcile aggressively later without double-charging or double-provisioning anyone.

Step 2: alert on missing volume, not just errors

The simplest useful detector compares the last hour against the same hour-of-week over the previous four weeks. Webhook traffic is usually seasonal, so a flat threshold either misses gaps at peak or cries wolf at 3 AM.

-- Postgres: sources whose last-hour volume fell below 30% of their hour-of-week baseline
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT provider, count(*) AS n
  FROM webhook_receipts
  WHERE source = 'push' AND received_at >= now() - interval '1 hour'
  GROUP BY provider
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT provider, count(*) / 4.0 AS avg_n
  FROM webhook_receipts
  WHERE source = 'push'
    AND received_at >= now() - interval '29 days'
    AND received_at <  now() - interval '1 day'
    AND extract(isodow FROM received_at) = extract(isodow FROM now())
    AND extract(hour   FROM received_at) = extract(hour   FROM now() - interval '1 hour')
  GROUP BY provider
)
SELECT b.provider, coalesce(r.n, 0) AS last_hour, round(b.avg_n, 1) AS expected
FROM baseline b
LEFT JOIN recent r USING (provider)
WHERE b.avg_n >= 5
  AND coalesce(r.n, 0) < b.avg_n * 0.3;

The avg_n >= 5 guard skips low-volume sources, where an empty hour is normal. For those, use a simpler "no events in N hours" rule, plus the reconciliation in step 3. Two more signals catch the "received but not processed" case and the rotated-secret case:

-- Stored but not processed for more than 15 minutes
SELECT provider, count(*) FROM webhook_receipts
WHERE processed_at IS NULL AND received_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
GROUP BY provider;

For signature rejections, count the stripe_webhook_rejected log line in your log platform and alert on any sustained non-zero rate.

Step 3: reconcile against the provider

Detection tells you something is wrong. Reconciliation repairs it without anyone replaying events by hand. Most providers offer either an events list or a way to fetch current object state. Stripe, for example, lets you list events from roughly the last 30 days.

// app/Console/Commands/ReconcileStripeEvents.php
public function handle(\Stripe\StripeClient $stripe): int
{
    $since = now()->subHours((int) $this->option('hours') ?: 6)->timestamp;
    $recovered = 0;

    $events = $stripe->events->all([
        'created' => ['gte' => $since],
        'types' => config('services.stripe.handled_events'),
        'limit' => 100,
    ]);

    foreach ($events->autoPagingIterator() as $event) {
        $inserted = DB::table('webhook_receipts')->insertOrIgnore([
            'provider' => 'stripe',
            'event_id' => $event->id,
            'event_type' => $event->type,
            'provider_created_at' => Carbon::createFromTimestamp($event->created),
            'source' => 'reconcile',
            'payload' => json_encode($event->toArray()),
        ]);
        if ($inserted) {
            ProcessWebhookReceipt::dispatch('stripe', $event->id);
            $recovered++;
        }
    }

    Log::info('stripe_reconcile', ['recovered' => $recovered, 'since' => $since]);
    return self::SUCCESS;
}

// routes/console.php
Schedule::command('webhooks:reconcile-stripe --hours=6')
    ->hourly()->onOneServer()->withoutOverlapping(30)
    ->pingOnSuccess(env('HB_STRIPE_RECONCILE_URL'));

The overlapping window (six hours, run hourly) means a short outage is covered several times. The recovered count is the most honest health metric you have: in a healthy system it is near zero. When it jumps, push delivery is broken even if nothing else looks wrong. And yes, the reconcile job itself gets a heartbeat, from Part 1.

If a provider has no events API, reconcile on state instead: page through the provider's subscriptions, orders or users updated since the last run and compare against your copies.

Choosing a strategy per provider

Provider capability Detection Reconciliation Notes
Events list API with IDs Volume baseline + recovered count Replay missed events by ID Best case; idempotent insert does the work
Object state API only Volume baseline Compare updated-since objects to local state Requires reliable updated_at filters
Delivery log with manual redeliver Volume baseline + provider dashboard checks Redeliver via API or UI Usually limited history; act quickly
No API at all "Silence for N hours" rule Periodic full export or manual review Document the risk with the business owner

Rolling it out

When we add this to a client system at Loop Origin, the order is: inventory every inbound webhook, add the receipts table and idempotent insert, wire the volume and unprocessed alerts, then add reconciliation for the integrations that touch money or access. If your stack needs this kind of plumbing, our custom web application development team designs integrations that assume delivery will fail, and our Laravel development service covers receivers, queues and reconciliation commands.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every inbound webhook source is listed with its owner and the events it should send.
  • [ ] Receipts are stored with a unique (provider, event_id) constraint before processing.
  • [ ] Signature failures are logged at warning level and alerted on.
  • [ ] Volume alerts compare against an hour-of-week baseline, not a fixed number.
  • [ ] Low-volume sources have a "no events in N hours" rule.
  • [ ] Stored-but-unprocessed receipts alert after a short window.
  • [ ] A scheduled reconciliation job exists for every money- or access-related integration.
  • [ ] The reconciliation job reports a recovered count and has its own heartbeat.
  • [ ] Provider notification emails go to a monitored shared inbox.
  • [ ] I tested the alerts by disabling a webhook endpoint in staging.

FAQ

Isn't reconciliation enough on its own?

It repairs data but adds delay equal to the reconcile interval. Push webhooks give speed; reconciliation gives correctness. You want both.

How far back should reconciliation look?

Several times the run interval, and never beyond what the provider retains. Hourly runs with a six-hour window are a practical default.

Will reconciled events be processed twice?

Not if processing keys off the unique event ID and handlers are idempotent. That is why the receipts table comes first.

What about event ordering?

Do not assume order. Handlers should fetch current object state or compare timestamps before applying older events.

Should I return 200 for events I do not handle?

Yes, after verifying the signature. Returning errors for unhandled types can lead providers to disable the endpoint.

How do I notice a disabled endpoint quickly?

The volume alert usually fires first. Also route provider account emails to a shared, monitored inbox, and check endpoint status in the provider dashboard during incident reviews.

    $inserted = DB::table('webhook_receipts')->insertOrIgnore([
        'provider' => 'stripe',
        'event_id' => $event->id,
        'event_type' => $event->type,
        'provider_created_at' => Carbon::createFromTimestamp($event->created),
        'payload' => json_encode($event->toArray()),
    ]);

    return response()->noContent();
}

The unique index makes duplicate deliveries and reconciliation overlaps harmless. That idempotency is what lets you reconcile aggressively later without double-charging or double-provisioning anyone.

Step 2: alert on missing volume, not just errors

The simplest useful detector compares the last hour against the same hour-of-week over the previous four weeks. Webhook traffic is usually seasonal, so a flat threshold either misses gaps at peak or cries wolf at 3 AM.

-- Postgres: sources whose last-hour volume fell below 30% of their hour-of-week baseline
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT provider, count(*) AS n
  FROM webhook_receipts
  WHERE source = 'push' AND received_at >= now() - interval '1 hour'
  GROUP BY provider
),
baseline AS (
  SELECT provider, count(*) / 4.0 AS avg_n
  FROM webhook_receipts
  WHERE source = 'push'
    AND received_at >= now() - interval '29 days'
    AND received_at <  now() - interval '1 day'
    AND extract(isodow FROM received_at) = extract(isodow FROM now())
    AND extract(hour   FROM received_at) = extract(hour   FROM now() - interval '1 hour')
  GROUP BY provider
)
SELECT b.provider, coalesce(r.n, 0) AS last_hour, round(b.avg_n, 1) AS expected
FROM baseline b
LEFT JOIN recent r USING (provider)
WHERE b.avg_n >= 5
  AND coalesce(r.n, 0) < b.avg_n * 0.3;

The avg_n >= 5 guard skips low-volume sources, where an empty hour is normal. For those, use a simpler "no events in N hours" rule, plus the reconciliation in step 3. Two more signals catch the "received but not processed" case and the rotated-secret case:

-- Stored but not processed for more than 15 minutes
SELECT provider, count(*) FROM webhook_receipts
WHERE processed_at IS NULL AND received_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
GROUP BY provider;

For signature rejections, count the stripe_webhook_rejected log line in your log platform and alert on any sustained non-zero rate.

Step 3: reconcile against the provider

Detection tells you something is wrong. Reconciliation repairs it without anyone replaying events by hand. Most providers offer either an events list or a way to fetch current object state. Stripe, for example, lets you list events from roughly the last 30 days.

// app/Console/Commands/ReconcileStripeEvents.php
public function handle(\Stripe\StripeClient $stripe): int
{
    $since = now()->subHours((int) $this->option('hours') ?: 6)->timestamp;
    $recovered = 0;

    $events = $stripe->events->all([
        'created' => ['gte' => $since],
        'types' => config('services.stripe.handled_events'),
        'limit' => 100,
    ]);

    foreach ($events->autoPagingIterator() as $event) {
        $inserted = DB::table('webhook_receipts')->insertOrIgnore([
            'provider' => 'stripe',
            'event_id' => $event->id,
            'event_type' => $event->type,
            'provider_created_at' => Carbon::createFromTimestamp($event->created),
            'source' => 'reconcile',
            'payload' => json_encode($event->toArray()),
        ]);
        if ($inserted) {
            ProcessWebhookReceipt::dispatch('stripe', $event->id);
            $recovered++;
        }
    }

    Log::info('stripe_reconcile', ['recovered' => $recovered, 'since' => $since]);
    return self::SUCCESS;
}

// routes/console.php
Schedule::command('webhooks:reconcile-stripe --hours=6')
    ->hourly()->onOneServer()->withoutOverlapping(30)
    ->pingOnSuccess(env('HB_STRIPE_RECONCILE_URL'));

The overlapping window (six hours, run hourly) means a short outage is covered several times. The recovered count is the most honest health metric you have: in a healthy system it is near zero. When it jumps, push delivery is broken even if nothing else looks wrong. And yes, the reconcile job itself gets a heartbeat, from Part 1.

If a provider has no events API, reconcile on state instead: page through the provider's subscriptions, orders or users updated since the last run and compare against your copies.

Choosing a strategy per provider

Provider capability Detection Reconciliation Notes
Events list API with IDs Volume baseline + recovered count Replay missed events by ID Best case; idempotent insert does the work
Object state API only Volume baseline Compare updated-since objects to local state Requires reliable updated_at filters
Delivery log with manual redeliver Volume baseline + provider dashboard checks Redeliver via API or UI Usually limited history; act quickly
No API at all "Silence for N hours" rule Periodic full export or manual review Document the risk with the business owner

Rolling it out

When we add this to a client system at Loop Origin, the order is: inventory every inbound webhook, add the receipts table and idempotent insert, wire the volume and unprocessed alerts, then add reconciliation for the integrations that touch money or access. If your stack needs this kind of plumbing, our custom web application development team designs integrations that assume delivery will fail, and our Laravel development service covers receivers, queues and reconciliation commands.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every inbound webhook source is listed with its owner and the events it should send.
  • [ ] Receipts are stored with a unique (provider, event_id) constraint before processing.
  • [ ] Signature failures are logged at warning level and alerted on.
  • [ ] Volume alerts compare against an hour-of-week baseline, not a fixed number.
  • [ ] Low-volume sources have a "no events in N hours" rule.
  • [ ] Stored-but-unprocessed receipts alert after a short window.
  • [ ] A scheduled reconciliation job exists for every money- or access-related integration.
  • [ ] The reconciliation job reports a recovered count and has its own heartbeat.
  • [ ] Provider notification emails go to a monitored shared inbox.
  • [ ] I tested the alerts by disabling a webhook endpoint in staging.

FAQ

Isn't reconciliation enough on its own?

It repairs data but adds delay equal to the reconcile interval. Push webhooks give speed; reconciliation gives correctness. You want both.

How far back should reconciliation look?

Several times the run interval, and never beyond what the provider retains. Hourly runs with a six-hour window are a practical default.

Will reconciled events be processed twice?

Not if processing keys off the unique event ID and handlers are idempotent. That is why the receipts table comes first.

What about event ordering?

Do not assume order. Handlers should fetch current object state or compare timestamps before applying older events.

Should I return 200 for events I do not handle?

Yes, after verifying the signature. Returning errors for unhandled types can lead providers to disable the endpoint.

How do I notice a disabled endpoint quickly?

The volume alert usually fires first. Also route provider account emails to a shared, monitored inbox, and check endpoint status in the provider dashboard during incident reviews.
