title: Rendering GitOps: how we built an ArgoCD repository with KCL
summary:
Our GitOps repository needed Go templates, Kustomize overlays, CUE schemas, and Python scripts just to make configuration changes reasonably safe. Even then, removing a redundant override could briefly trigger a downgrade. We decided to rethink how we assembled our Argo CD applications, using KCL to generate and validate their definitions before they reached the cluster. In this post, I walk through the component model we built, how it changed our review workflow, and where the additional machinery earns its keep.

The pain we started from

Our GitOps repository had a component directory per deployment unit, a Kustomize overlay per platform, and one ApplicationSet per component. Each platform patched the Git file generator so that Go templates could read its configuration:

destination:
  namespace: "team-widget-{{ .platform.env }}"
syncOptions:
  - ApplyOutOfSyncOnly={{ dig "components" "widget" "syncOptions" "ApplyOutOfSyncOnly" "true" . }}

This worked, but understanding a change meant mentally evaluating templates, platform values, and defaults. The files we reviewed were the inputs to an Application, rather than the Application itself.

Initially, we only saw the generated result after a change landed on main and the controllers reconciled it. We added CUE schemas and Python scripts to check that configuration was valid and that the dig lookups resolved. Eventually, we also built a pipeline that asked Argo CD to render changes before merging and posted the diff on the pull request.

That improved visibility, but the feedback loop could take tens of minutes. We had assembled several technologies and a cluster-dependent workflow to make one abstraction trustworthy.

There was another problem that validation alone did not solve.

When a cleanup becomes a downgrade

Suppose a component defaults to version 1, but a platform overrides it to version 2. Once every platform uses version 2, we update the component default and remove the overrides. This should leave the resulting applications unchanged.

In our setup, however, the ApplicationSet template and the platform configuration used by its Git generator were updated through separate reconciliation paths. We observed a sequence where the generator picked up the removal of an override before the controller received the updated template. The controller temporarily combined the new platform configuration with the old default, generating an Application pointing back to version 1.

With automated sync, that could trigger a downgrade, followed by another upgrade once the remaining configuration caught up.

This was a consequence of how we assembled and reconciled those inputs. The Git generator documentation describes polling and revision-cache behavior, but the important point for our design was simpler: we wanted to resolve component defaults and platform overrides together, before either reached the cluster.

The design

We replaced the ApplicationSet templates with a small KCL module. Its model has two parts:

  • Components describe a deployment unit: one or more related Helm charts, their defaults, and the settings shared across platforms.
  • Platforms select the components to deploy to a Kubernetes cluster and specify the differences from those defaults.

A render step turns each platform definition into concrete Argo CD Application resources. CI writes those resources to manifests//, which is the configuration Argo CD consumes.

There are still two rendering stages. KCL generates the Application definitions before deployment. Argo CD then renders the Helm charts referenced by those applications and reconciles their resources. We moved the composition of applications out of the cluster; we kept Helm rendering in Argo CD.

This applies the rendered manifests pattern to the application-definition layer. We do not store the final Helm-generated workload manifests in Git.

Components: the typed vocabulary

A component is a value in a KCL package. It holds the defaults that should be shared across platforms: chart revisions, Helm release-name settings, values, namespace prefixes, sync policy, and labels.

# components/web/widget.k
import file
import yaml

import ..lib as lib

widget = lib.Component {
    name = "web/widget"
    namespacePrefix = "team-widget-"
    charts = [
        lib.Chart {
            name = "acme/widget"
            version = "acme/widget/v1.4.2"
            releaseName = "widget"
            values = yaml.decode(file.read("widget.values.yaml"))
        }
        lib.Chart {
            name = "acme/widget-sidecar"
            version = "acme/widget-sidecar/v0.3.0"
            releaseName = "widget-sidecar"
        }
    ]
}

The version strings follow our repository's chart-tag convention. They identify the revision of the chart source, separately from any container image tag supplied through Helm values.

A component can contain more than one chart when those charts belong to the same deployment unit. Each chart becomes one source in the resulting Application. They therefore share an Argo CD application lifecycle. This is useful for closely related charts, but would be an awkward way to group otherwise independent applications.

Although we configure a releaseName for each Helm source, Argo CD manages the deployed resources itself. It uses Helm to generate manifests, rather than managing ordinary Helm releases.

There is no separate component registry to maintain. A component is a top-level variable, and a platform refers to it by symbol, such as web.widget.

Platforms: explicit differences

A platform directory contains a platform.k file with its name, environment, selected components, and chart overrides. Values that differ from the component defaults live in YAML files next to it:

# platforms/p-north-01/platform.k
import ...components as gitops
import ...components.core as core
import ...components.web as web

import file
import yaml

name = "p-north-01"
env = "d"

applications = gitops.manifests(name, env, [
    {
        component = web.widget
        charts = [
            {
                name = "acme/widget"
                values = yaml.decode(file.read("widget.values.override.yaml"))
            }
        ]
    }
    {
        component = core.queue
        charts = [
            {
                name = "acme/queue"
                version = "acme/queue/v2.0.0"
            }
        ]
    }
])

# platforms/p-north-01/widget.values.override.yaml
image:
  tag: v1.4.2-rc1

Here, the widget override selects its chart by name and changes a container image tag through its values. The queue override changes the chart revision itself. These are independent choices.

The split is deliberate: components define shared defaults, while platforms state their exceptions. Rolling out a new default means editing the component. Keeping one platform on a different revision means setting the override there.

The render step

manifests() takes the platform name, environment, and application definitions. It combines the component defaults with platform overrides and constructs the Argo CD objects.

We use generated Argo CD models from the KCL community modules, rather than maintaining the Application schema ourselves. Our own schemas describe the higher-level component and platform inputs; the imported schemas describe the output resources.

We generate the set of Application resources:

# components/manifests.k
import argo_cd.v1alpha1.argoproj_io_v1alpha1_application as argo
# some code is omitted...

# one ArgoCD source per chart of the component, with the platform's overrides
source = lambda chart: Chart, overrides: [ChartOverride] -> any {
    override = overrides[0] if overrides else {}

    # the union re-evaluates the derived attributes, so `version_is_tag` is about
    # the effective version
    effective = chart | {
        **({"version" = override.version} if override.version else {})
        **({"releaseName" = override.releaseName} if override.releaseName else {})
    }

    values = {**chart.values, **override.values}

    {
        repoURL: effective.repoURL
        path: effective.path
        targetRevision: effective.version
        helm = {
            releaseName = effective.releaseName
            **({"valuesObject" = values} if values else {})
        }
    }
}

# NB: no local may be called `name`, dict literal keys shadow it
application = lambda app: Application, platform: str, env: str -> argo.Application {
    component = app.component
    application_name = app.name or component.name.replace("/", "-")

    chart_names = [c.name for c in component.charts]
    unnamed = [o for o in app.charts if not o.name]
    assert len(unnamed) == 0 or len(component.charts) == 1, "component '${component.name}' has ${len(component.charts)} charts, so an override has to set 'name'"
    unknown = [o.name for o in app.charts if o.name and o.name not in chart_names]
    assert len(unknown) == 0, "component '${component.name}' has no chart ${unknown}, it has ${chart_names}"

    argo.Application {
        metadata = {
           # some more code...
        }
        spec = {
            project = component.project
            destination = {
                server = "https://kubernetes.default.svc"
                namespace = (app.namespacePrefix or component.namespacePrefix) + env
            }
            syncPolicy = {
                automated = {
                    selfHeal = component.syncPolicy.selfHeal
                    prune = component.syncPolicy.prune
                } if component.syncPolicy.automated else Undefined
                syncOptions = component.syncPolicy.syncOptions
            }
            revisionHistoryLimit = component.revisionHistoryLimit
            sources = [source(c, overrides_of(app, c)) for c in component.charts]
        }
    }
}

and them dump them to files:

MANIFESTS_DIR = option("manifests_dir") or "manifests"

# Write one YAML file per application to `manifests//.yaml`,
# so that a plain `kcl run` of a platform dumps its manifests.
dump = lambda platform: str, applications: [any] -> bool {
    dir = file.modpath() + "/" + MANIFESTS_DIR + "/" + platform
    _created = file.mkdir(dir)
    _written = [yaml.dump_to_file(a, dir + "/" + a.metadata.name + ".yaml") for a in applications]
    True
}

manifests = lambda {
    platform: str,
    env: str,
    applications: [lib.Application],
} -> [argo.Application] {
    assert regex.match(platform, r"^[a-z]-[a-z0-9-]+$"), "platform name '${platform}' must look like '-', e.g. p- or c-"
    assert regex.match(env, r"^[a-z]$"), "env '${env}' must be a short lowercase environment letter"

    rendered = [lib.application(app, platform, env) for app in applications]
    names = [a.metadata.name for a in rendered]
    duplicates = [n for n in names if len([m for m in names if m == n]) > 1]
    assert len(duplicates) == 0, "duplicate application name(s) ${duplicates}"

    _dumped = output.dump(platform, rendered)
    rendered
}

The renderer writes one file per application to manifests//.yaml. Each file contains the resolved application definition, including its destination, source revisions, and values. Argo CD no longer needs to reconstruct that definition from an ApplicationSet template and separately refreshed platform configuration.

For the earlier default-and-override cleanup, this gives us a useful property: both inputs are evaluated together from the same source checkout. If the resolved application has not changed, its generated YAML does not change either. This removes the mixed-input failure we encountered; it does not make deployment across multiple applications atomic.

What changed for us

The model catches mistakes before deployment

The type system makes the configuration easier to navigate. Component references are symbols, schemas document the available fields, and mistakes can produce diagnostics close to the input that caused them:

error[E2L23]: CompileError
Cannot add member 'componnt' to schema 'Application', did you mean '["component"]'?

Our own checks also catch mistakes that are structurally valid but meaningless in the model. An override targeting a nonexistent chart produces an error such as:

component 'infra/docs' has no chart [acme/doc], it has [acme/docs, acme/permission-sync]

That is much more useful than finding out later that a configuration change did nothing.

KCL's check blocks and assertions let us keep configuration rules next to the schemas they constrain. For example, we check that namespace prefixes end with -, because we append the environment letter, and that application names are unique within a platform. We also require distinct release-name settings within a component as a naming safeguard, although that alone cannot prove the charts generate distinct Kubernetes resources.

Not every rule is an error. We warn when a chart revision does not follow our tag convention, because we occasionally deploy a branch deliberately. That warning checks our convention; it does not establish that the referenced revision exists.

These checks cover the model we have defined. They do not automatically validate every key in a YAML values file against the corresponding chart. The generated Application schema knows about helm.valuesObject, but chart-specific values need their own validation. Helm rendering and deployment can still fail for reasons outside our KCL model.

Reviewing the result becomes a local operation

Our diff command re-renders every platform into a scratch directory and compares the generated application definitions with the committed output. A reviewer can see which applications change, which source revisions move, and which values or sync settings differ.

On our repository, local generation takes a few hundred milliseconds on a laptop. That timing covers KCL generation of the application resources. It excludes chart downloads, Helm rendering, and comparison with live cluster state.

Previously, getting feedback meant pushing a change and waiting for the pipeline to ask Argo CD to render it. That complete loop could take tens of minutes. Now we can inspect the application-definition delta locally before pushing anything, and CI posts that delta on the pull request.

The distinction matters: a changed Helm value appears in this diff, but the resulting change to a Deployment does not. We can review the exact application configuration we intend to publish without claiming that we have already inspected every workload it will produce.

The pipeline owns the generated files

Contributors edit components, platform definitions, and values files. They do not edit manifests/ directly; a check rejects those changes. The pull request contains the source changes, and the generated delta is available in its review comments.

After merge, a second pipeline renders the repository and commits the generated applications. Argo CD then picks them up. Generating and committing the output is part of the delivery process, rather than a step someone has to remember locally.

This also gives us two things to inspect when something goes wrong: the source configuration that expressed the change and the generated Application that was published.

What we still own

Moving generation into CI adds responsibility there. We maintain the component model, rendering and diff scripts, and the check protecting the generated directory. The supporting shell scripts and KCL amount to a few hundred lines, but line count is only part of the maintenance cost.

The publication step is now part of the deployment path. If it fails after merge, the generated configuration remains behind the source configuration. Concurrent runs also need care: an older render must not overwrite output from a newer change. Reproducibility requires keeping the KCL toolchain and model dependencies under control, including the generated types for the Argo CD version we run.

KCL is also less familiar to most engineers than YAML or Helm. Its syntax will feel familiar to people who know Python, but learning the language and understanding our model still takes time. We have replaced a collection of abstractions with one we find easier to reason about; we still have an abstraction to maintain.

Finally, there are useful failure modes this design does not eliminate. A valid Application can reference an unavailable chart revision. Helm can reject values or generate resources that the target cluster will not accept. Cluster policy still has a role, especially for changes that do not pass through this repository.

Why KCL?

Generating applications before deployment does not require KCL. We could have invested further in evaluating the existing templates locally, or built a similar model using another configuration language.

What we appreciate about KCL is that the abstractions, types, constraints, and output construction live together. We no longer need Go templates for the application definitions, CUE for their input schemas, and Python to check the relationship between them.

The two decisions solve related problems: generating before deployment makes application definitions inspectable, while KCL gives us a way to express and validate how those definitions are assembled.

For a small repository with straightforward applications, maintaining this model might cost more than it saves. For us, the repeated platform configuration, shared defaults, and existing validation machinery made the trade-off worthwhile.

Day to day

A change now looks like this: edit a component or platform, run the formatter and checks, inspect the generated application delta, and open a pull request. CI posts the same kind of delta for the reviewer. Once the change is merged, the publication pipeline updates the generated applications and Argo CD reconciles them.

Argo CD still does important work, including rendering Helm charts. It no longer has to assemble our application definitions from several layers of templates and platform configuration. That is a smaller responsibility, and one we find much easier to debug.

Closing thoughts

The most useful change was making the resolved application definition something we could inspect before deployment. KCL gave us a typed model for producing it, with constraints that describe how our repository is supposed to work.

If your GitOps repository has accumulated ApplicationSet templates, dig lookups, overlay patches, and separate validation scripts, this approach is worth exploring. Start with one deployment unit, generate its Application alongside the existing setup, and compare the result. That will tell you more about whether the model fits your repository than migrating everything at once.

And if you want the longer argument for why a compiled, constraint-based language fits platform engineering, I wrote about that here.

# one ArgoCD source per chart of the component, with the platform's overrides

    override = overrides[0] if overrides else {}

    # the union re-evaluates the derived attributes, so `version_is_tag` is about
    # the effective version
    effective = chart | {
        **({"version" = override.version} if override.version else {})
        **({"releaseName" = override.releaseName} if override.releaseName else {})
    }

    application_name = app.name or component.name.replace("/", "-")

This removes the mixed-input failure we encountered; it does not make deployment across multiple applications atomic.

What changed for us

The model catches mistakes before deployment

The type system makes the configuration easier to navigate. Component references are symbols, schemas document the available fields, and mistakes can produce diagnostics close to the input that caused them:

error[E2L23]: CompileError
Cannot add member 'componnt' to schema 'Application', did you mean '["component"]'?

Our own checks also catch mistakes that are structurally valid but meaningless in the model. An override targeting a nonexistent chart produces an error such as:

component 'infra/docs' has no chart [acme/doc], it has [acme/docs, acme/permission-sync]

That is much more useful than finding out later that a configuration change did nothing.

KCL's check blocks and assertions let us keep configuration rules next to the schemas they constrain. For example, we check that namespace prefixes end with -, because we append the environment letter, and that application names are unique within a platform. We also require distinct release-name settings within a component as a naming safeguard, although that alone cannot prove the charts generate distinct Kubernetes resources.

Not every rule is an error. We warn when a chart revision does not follow our tag convention, because we occasionally deploy a branch deliberately. That warning checks our convention; it does not establish that the referenced revision exists.

These checks cover the model we have defined. They do not automatically validate every key in a YAML values file against the corresponding chart. The generated Application schema knows about helm.valuesObject, but chart-specific values need their own validation. Helm rendering and deployment can still fail for reasons outside our KCL model.

Reviewing the result becomes a local operation

Our diff command re-renders every platform into a scratch directory and compares the generated application definitions with the committed output. A reviewer can see which applications change, which source revisions move, and which values or sync settings differ.

On our repository, local generation takes a few hundred milliseconds on a laptop. That timing covers KCL generation of the application resources. It excludes chart downloads, Helm rendering, and comparison with live cluster state.

Previously, getting feedback meant pushing a change and waiting for the pipeline to ask Argo CD to render it. That complete loop could take tens of minutes. Now we can inspect the application-definition delta locally before pushing anything, and CI posts that delta on the pull request.

The distinction matters: a changed Helm value appears in this diff, but the resulting change to a Deployment does not. We can review the exact application configuration we intend to publish without claiming that we have already inspected every workload it will produce.

The pipeline owns the generated files

Contributors edit components, platform definitions, and values files. They do not edit manifests/ directly; a check rejects those changes. The pull request contains the source changes, and the generated delta is available in its review comments.

After merge, a second pipeline renders the repository and commits the generated applications. Argo CD then picks them up. Generating and committing the output is part of the delivery process, rather than a step someone has to remember locally.

This also gives us two things to inspect when something goes wrong: the source configuration that expressed the change and the generated Application that was published.

What we still own

Moving generation into CI adds responsibility there. We maintain the component model, rendering and diff scripts, and the check protecting the generated directory. The supporting shell scripts and KCL amount to a few hundred lines, but line count is only part of the maintenance cost.

The publication step is now part of the deployment path. If it fails after merge, the generated configuration remains behind the source configuration. Concurrent runs also need care: an older render must not overwrite output from a newer change. Reproducibility requires keeping the KCL toolchain and model dependencies under control, including the generated types for the Argo CD version we run.

KCL is also less familiar to most engineers than YAML or Helm. Its syntax will feel familiar to people who know Python, but learning the language and understanding our model still takes time. We have replaced a collection of abstractions with one we find easier to reason about; we still have an abstraction to maintain.

Finally, there are useful failure modes this design does not eliminate. A valid Application can reference an unavailable chart revision. Helm can reject values or generate resources that the target cluster will not accept. Cluster policy still has a role, especially for changes that do not pass through this repository.

Why KCL?

Generating applications before deployment does not require KCL. We could have invested further in evaluating the existing templates locally, or built a similar model using another configuration language.

What we appreciate about KCL is that the abstractions, types, constraints, and output construction live together. We no longer need Go templates for the application definitions, CUE for their input schemas, and Python to check the relationship between them.

The two decisions solve related problems: generating before deployment makes application definitions inspectable, while KCL gives us a way to express and validate how those definitions are assembled.

For a small repository with straightforward applications, maintaining this model might cost more than it saves. For us, the repeated platform configuration, shared defaults, and existing validation machinery made the trade-off worthwhile.

Day to day

A change now looks like this: edit a component or platform, run the formatter and checks, inspect the generated application delta, and open a pull request. CI posts the same kind of delta for the reviewer. Once the change is merged, the publication pipeline updates the generated applications and Argo CD reconciles them.

Argo CD still does important work, including rendering Helm charts. It no longer has to assemble our application definitions from several layers of templates and platform configuration. That is a smaller responsibility, and one we find much easier to debug.

Closing thoughts

The most useful change was making the resolved application definition something we could inspect before deployment. KCL gave us a typed model for producing it, with constraints that describe how our repository is supposed to work.

If your GitOps repository has accumulated ApplicationSet templates, dig lookups, overlay patches, and separate validation scripts, this approach is worth exploring. Start with one deployment unit, generate its Application alongside the existing setup, and compare the result. That will tell you more about whether the model fits your repository than migrating everything at once.

And if you want the longer argument for why a compiled, constraint-based language fits platform engineering, I wrote about that here.

title: How I Run Multiple AI Coding Agents Across Multiple Repositories, and Git Branches Simultaneously
summary:
Running multiple AI coding agents across separate repositories and Git branches simultaneously requires moving away from traditional IDE sidebar panels toward a terminal-native Agentic Development Environment (ADE) like Warp 2.0. By combining multi-session block interfaces, native Git worktree isolation, and multi-agent orchestration, developers can delegate concurrent tasks to different AI models (such as Warp Agent, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex) while maintaining independent state across each repository. However, executing parallel AI sessions locally imposes noticeable CPU and memory hardware demands and requires strict directory boundaries to avoid Git lock collisions.

Industry Adoption and Benchmark Metrics

The shift toward terminal-centric agentic workspaces is supported by performance benchmarks and rapid developer adoption metrics.

Warp Agent demonstrates strong autonomous coding execution, scoring 52% on Terminal-Bench (ranking #1 overall) and 71% on SWE-bench Verified (ranking in the top 5 overall). This performance reflects its ability to navigate terminal environments, execute diagnostic commands, and self-correct syntax errors during execution.

In terms of open-source ecosystem momentum, Warp released its Rust client application under the AGPLv3 license, generating over 52,000 GitHub stars shortly after launch. As engineering teams move away from manual line typing, terminal environments that offer native worktree parsing and structured block logging are becoming standard infrastructure for high-velocity software delivery.

The IDE Sidebar Bottleneck in the Agentic Era

Modern software engineering frequently requires managing microservice architectures, multi-package monorepos, or distributed backend systems. A single user feature might touch a React web client, a Node.js API gateway, a Go background worker, and a shared data validation utility. As development workflow shifts from writing raw code line-by-line to orchestrating autonomous AI agents, standard integrated development environments reveal a fundamental structural bottleneck.

Traditional IDEs reserve 80 to 85 percent of screen real estate for static text editors. AI coding assistants are relegated to narrow sidebar chat windows or floating popups. When an engineer attempts to coordinate AI-driven feature development across three distinct microservices, standard IDEs force sequential tab-switching, context stashing, and constant manual directory navigation. Industry analysis indicates nearly 90 percent of code generated in agentic workflows originates from prompt interactions rather than direct editor typing. Forcing these high-bandwidth interactions into secondary sidebars creates cognitive friction and stalls parallel execution.

Furthermore, context switching within a single repository directory causes severe operational friction. Switching Git branches to let an agent work on a hotfix stashes uncommitted work, interrupts local test runners, and scrambles the memory context of active language servers. To unlock true parallel delivery, developer workspaces must evolve to support multi-threaded task execution across isolated code environments.

Core Architecture: Worktree Isolation and Multi-Agent Orchestration

Warp 2.0 addresses these structural limits by redesigning the developer environment as an Agentic Development Environment (ADE). Instead of centering the screen on a static text document, Warp treats terminal command outputs, AI prompt interactions, and execution logs as first-class workspace blocks.

The fundamental architecture relies on three primary subsystems:

  1. Native Git Worktree Isolation: Rather than checking out different branches within the same directory, Git worktrees allow multiple branch checkouts (main, feature-auth, bugfix-gateway) into separate physical folders linked to a single Git repository. Warp 2.0 natively parses .git pointers inside worktrees, running background code indexers, branch status chips, and diff viewers independently for each folder.
  2. Multi-Threaded Agent Orchestration: Developers can run heterogeneous agent stacks simultaneously across workspace tabs or split panes. A developer can run Claude Code in one terminal pane for complex logic refactoring, Gemini CLI in another for massive context processing, and Warp Agent for shell command execution.
  3. Dedicated Code Review Panels and Permission Guardrails: As agents execute code autonomously, Warp provides per-session Code Review panels that display uncommitted diffs hunk-by-hunk. Security guardrails, including repository-level AGENTS.md rules and command deny lists, prevent agents from executing destructive terminal commands such as unapproved force pushes or directory deletions. 
[Repository A: Frontend] ──> Git Worktree A ──> Warp Tab 1 (Warp Agent: UI Feature)
                                                     │
[Repository B: Backend]  ──> Git Worktree B ──> Warp Tab 2 (Claude Code: API Setup) ──> Unified Notification
                                                     │                                     & Code Review Panel
[Repository C: Shared]   ──> Main Directory ──> Warp Tab 3 (Codex CLI: Test Suite)

Step-by-Step Practical Framework: Running Parallel Agents

Setting up a multi-repository, multi-agent workflow in Warp 2.0 involves structured execution steps to ensure complete task isolation.

Step 1: Establish Workspace Layout and Git Worktrees

Create isolated worktree directories for active feature branches so agents never collide in the same folder:

cd ~/projects/backend-service
git worktree add ../backend-feature-oauth feature/oauth-setup

Open Warp 2.0, create a new Workspace, and open three dedicated terminal tabs or split panes:

  • Tab 1: Frontend repository (~/projects/frontend-app)
  • Tab 2: Backend worktree (~/projects/backend-feature-oauth)
  • Tab 3: Shared utilities (~/projects/core-utils)

Step 2: Configure Permission Guardrails and Voice Input

Create an AGENTS.md file in each repository root to define architectural rules, test execution commands, and forbidden operations. Enable Warp command deny lists to block destructive commands (rm -rf *, git push --force).

To accelerate prompt construction across multiple sessions, leverage hands-free voice input within Warp's prompt box to dictate complex context and architectural requirements directly to the target agent without typing.

Step 3: Delegate Parallel Tasks Across Repositories and Branches

Assign discrete tasks to parallel agents across your open tabs:

  • Tab 1 (Frontend App): Dictate or prompt Warp Agent: "Build an OAuth login modal component using our existing design tokens in /components/auth. Execute npm test when complete."
  • Tab 2 (Backend Worktree): Launch Claude Code CLI: "Implement OAuth2 JWT validation endpoints in src/controllers/auth.ts. Write comprehensive unit tests in tests/auth.test.ts."
  • Tab 3 (Shared Utilities): Launch Codex CLI: "Refactor token validation helpers for UTF-8 compliance while maintaining backward compatibility."

Step 4: Monitor Execution and Review Diffs

Observe status indicators across the Warp workspace header. When an agent moves from RUNNING to NEEDS_INPUT or SUCCEEDED, click the session block to inspect output. Open Warp's built-in Code Review panel in each tab to audit generated diffs, revert unwanted hunk modifications, and commit verified changes.

Trade-offs, Resource Limits, and Security Guardrails

While parallel multi-agent execution dramatically accelerates delivery, developers must account for clear operational trade-offs:

  • Workstation Hardware Overhead: Running multiple LLM CLI agents simultaneously creates high CPU and memory demand. Each active agent process runs background file watchers, language server protocol (LSP) instances, and workspace embeddings. Workstations with 16GB RAM can experience performance degradation when executing more than three concurrent local agent sessions.
  • Directory Collisions: Assigning multiple agents to the same branch within a single working directory causes severe file overwrite collisions and Git index lock errors (.git/index.lock). Strict Git worktree usage or separate repository paths are mandatory.
  • Context Drift: In extended agent sessions exceeding 30 conversation turns, LLM context windows can compress, causing agents to drift from original architectural guidelines or reference deprecated APIs. Spawning fresh agent sessions for discrete sub-tasks mitigates this degradation.
  • Enterprise Telemetry and Privacy: While Warp's desktop client is open-source, server-side orchestration platforms and hosted AI models route data through external APIs. Enterprises operating under zero-retention compliance policies must configure explicit data retention rules and model routing options.

Summary Checklist and Next Steps

  • Transition multi-repo workflows from IDE sidebars to terminal workspaces using Warp 2.0.
  • Isolate parallel feature branches using Git worktrees (git worktree add) to prevent file overwrite collisions.
  • Establish repository guardrails using AGENTS.md files and command deny lists to safely run autonomous CLI agents.
  • Monitor multi-agent session lifecycle states (RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, NEEDS_INPUT) via Warp's visual block interface.
  • Audit generated changes using per-session Code Review panels before committing code.

  • Warp Official Documentation: Git worktrees
  • Introducing Warp 2.0: Reimagining coding with the Agentic Development Environment
  • Managing Multiple AI Coding Agents in Warp Terminal: A Complete Guide
  • Warp Open-Source Client Repository

title: Workspace is not a cloud desktop: four things it does not restore
summary:
I work on CloudGPU, so read this as a note from the people who build it.

CloudGPU recently added Workspace: you can save project files independently of a GPU, pin them as an immutable version, and restore that version into a later Job or onto a GPU you are already renting. The most common misreading we see is "so it is a cloud desktop now". It is not, and designing around that difference saves real time.

Here are the four things Workspace does not bring back, and what to do about each.

1. Your operating system, drivers and installed packages

A Workspace version is a manifest: relative project paths mapped to files you uploaded and completed. When a Job starts with workspace_version_id, those files are restored into a fresh project directory before your command runs. That is all.

The machine underneath is whatever template the new Job or instance uses. pip install results, a compiled extension, a CUDA build you fixed by hand last week: none of that is in the version.

What to do: keep environment setup as code inside the project. A setup.sh or a pinned requirements.txt / environment.yml that your Job command runs first is the version-controlled replacement for "the machine I had".

# Job command: rebuild the environment, then run
bash setup.sh && python render.py --config configs/shot_014.yaml

2. Changes you made after saving

A version is immutable. If you edit configs/shot_014.yaml on a running GPU, the saved version still holds the old file. Nothing syncs back automatically.

What to do: treat "save a new version" as an explicit step, the same way you treat git commit. Name it after what changed (shot014-fix-lighting), not after the date.

3. Job outputs

The platform does not collect outputs for you. A Job runs one command, and the local storage of that Job's GPU is erased when it ends. If the command did not export its results, they are gone, even if the Job "succeeded".

What to do: make export part of the command, and check it as an acceptance step:

python render.py --out out/ \
  && ls out/*.png | wc -l \
  && for out/>

Then verify on your side that the expected number of files arrived and that they open. A zero exit code is not proof that usable files reached you.

4. Unlimited time and unlimited space

Saved files are subject to account eligibility, a quota and a retention policy. Completed files carry an expires_at; downloading a file does not renew it, and a version that contains an expired file becomes unusable. Storage charges are separate from the max_spend_usd cap on a GPU Job, and a budget-limited agent key cannot switch on paid storage.

What to do: read your own limits from the authenticated GET /v1/storage before you plan a long project, and keep your own copy of anything you cannot afford to lose.

So what is it good for?

Three patterns where it genuinely helps:

  • Repeatable runs. Pass the same workspace_version_id to two Jobs and you know both started from byte-identical project files. If the outputs differ, the cause is elsewhere (seed, environment, upstream model), which narrows the search.
  • Picking up on a GPU you already rent. A saved version can be applied to a running instance. It lands in a new private directory, does not overwrite your existing files, and does not install anything, run anything or restart the GPU. You decide what happens next.
  • Handing a project to an agent. An agent with its own scoped key can start a Job from a version without you uploading files again in every session.

A quick mental model

Layer Survives the GPU? Who is responsible
OS, drivers, packages No Your setup script
Project files you saved as a version Yes, within quota and retention Workspace
Edits after the save No, until you save a new version You
Job outputs No, unless exported Your Job command

A short overview

If you have never seen CloudGPU, this short video shows what it is in general terms (it is not a Workspace tutorial):

Read more

  • Agent and persistence API docs: https://cloudgpu.app/docs/agents?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg04_codingagent&utm_content=pack1109gf_devto_workspace_boundary
  • Check whether persistence is enabled: GET https://cloudgpu.app/v1/public/compute-capabilities

Eligibility and full terms: https://cloudgpu.app/terms?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=202611_seg04_codingagent&utm_content=pack1109gf_devto_workspace_boundary

What does your team keep outside the GPU today: a setup script, a container image, or something else? I am curious which part breaks most often.

The most common misreading we see is "so it is a cloud desktop now". It is not, and designing around that difference saves real time.

Here are the four things Workspace does not bring back, and what to do about each.

1. Your operating system, drivers and installed packages

A Workspace version is a manifest: relative project paths mapped to files you uploaded and completed. When a Job starts with workspace_version_id, those files are restored into a fresh project directory before your command runs. That is all.

The machine underneath is whatever template the new Job or instance uses. pip install results, a compiled extension, a CUDA build you fixed by hand last week: none of that is in the version.

What to do: keep environment setup as code inside the project. A setup.sh or a pinned requirements.txt / environment.yml that your Job command runs first is the version-controlled replacement for "the machine I had".

# Job command: rebuild the environment, then run
bash setup.sh && python render.py --config configs/shot_014.yaml

2. Changes you made after saving

A version is immutable. If you edit configs/shot_014.yaml on a running GPU, the saved version still holds the old file. Nothing syncs back automatically.

What to do: treat "save a new version" as an explicit step, the same way you treat git commit. Name it after what changed (shot014-fix-lighting), not after the date.

3. Job outputs

The platform does not collect outputs for you. A Job runs one command, and the local storage of that Job's GPU is erased when it ends. If the command did not export its results, they are gone, even if the Job "succeeded".

What to do: make export part of the command, and check it as an acceptance step:

python render.py --out out/ \
  && ls out/*.png | wc -l \
  && for out/>

Then verify on your side that the expected number of files arrived and that they open. A zero exit code is not proof that usable files reached you.

4. Unlimited time and unlimited space

Saved files are subject to account eligibility, a quota and a retention policy. Completed files carry an expires_at; downloading a file does not renew it, and a version that contains an expired file becomes unusable. Storage charges are separate from the max_spend_usd cap on a GPU Job, and a budget-limited agent key cannot switch on paid storage.

What to do: read your own limits from the authenticated GET /v1/storage before you plan a long project, and keep your own copy of anything you cannot afford to lose.

So what is it good for?

Three patterns where it genuinely helps:

  • Repeatable runs. Pass the same workspace_version_id to two Jobs and you know both started from byte-identical project files. If the outputs differ, the cause is elsewhere (seed, environment, upstream model), which narrows the search.
  • Picking up on a GPU you already rent. A saved version can be applied to a running instance. It lands in a new private directory, does not overwrite your existing files, and does not install anything, run anything or restart the GPU. You decide what happens next.
  • Handing a project to an agent. An agent with its own scoped key can start a Job from a version without you uploading files again in every session.

A quick mental model

Layer Survives the GPU? Who is responsible
OS, drivers, packages No Your setup script
Project files you saved as a version Yes, within quota and retention Workspace
Edits after the save No, until you save a new version You
Job outputs No, unless exported Your Job command

A short overview

If you have never seen CloudGPU, this short video shows what it is in general terms (it is not a Workspace tutorial):

title: Building a Terminology Pipeline for Multilingual Pitch Decks (Before Your Series A Blows Up)
summary:
A startup I worked with raised a seed round in Lisbon, then went to raise a Series A from a UK fund. Same company, same numbers, same traction. Three different people translated three different documents (the deck, the financial model notes, and the term sheet summary) over three weeks, with no shared glossary. The result: "receita" became "revenue" in one file and "turnover" in another, ARR was calculated two different ways in the deck versus the model, and the investor's associate flagged it in the first due diligence call.

Nobody lost the round over this, but it cost a week of clarifying emails during a period when speed matters more than almost anything else. The source article on pitch deck translation for funding rounds covers why this happens from a linguistic and financial-register perspective. This post covers it from the other side: how to build a pipeline so it doesn't happen to your documents, using tools you probably already have access to.

The actual problem is version control, not translation quality

Treat a pitch deck, a financial model, a term sheet and a data room as what they actually are: a distributed system with no single source of truth for terminology. Every document is edited independently, often by different people, often under deadline pressure, and nothing enforces consistency between them.

This is a solved problem in software. We just don't usually apply the solution to fundraising docs.

Step 1: build a glossary as a structured data file, not a spreadsheet tab

Skip the shared Google Sheet that three people forget to check. Define your glossary as a JSON or YAML file that lives in version control alongside your docs.

# glossary.yml
terms:
  - source: "receita recorrente mensal"
    target_en: "MRR"
    context: "financial_metric"
    do_not_translate_as: ["monthly recurring income", "monthly revenue"]
  - source: "taxa de queima"
    target_en: "burn rate"
    context: "financial_metric"
  - source: "pré-money"
    target_en: "pre-money valuation"
    context: "cap_table"
  - source: "quadro de capital"
    target_en: "cap table"
    context: "cap_table"

This gives you something machines and humans can both check against. Translators (human or AI-assisted) get an authoritative reference. You get something you can lint.

Step 2: lint your documents against the glossary

If your deck and financial model exist as Markdown, plain text exports, or even extracted PDF text, you can write a basic consistency checker in a few lines:

import yaml
import re

def load_glossary(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return yaml.safe_load(f)["terms"]

def check_consistency(doc_text, glossary):
    issues = []
    for term in glossary:
        forbidden = term.get("do_not_translate_as", [])
        for bad_phrase in forbidden:
            if re.search(bad_phrase, doc_text, re.IGNORECASE):
                issues.append(
                    f"Found '{bad_phrase}', expected '{term['target_en']}'"
                )
    return issues

glossary = load_glossary("glossary.yml")
with open("financial_model_notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()

for issue in check_consistency(text, glossary):
    print(issue)

This is intentionally simple. You can extend it with fuzzy matching, number format validation (comma vs. period decimal separators are a real recurring bug, not a nitpick), or plug it into a CI step that runs every time someone updates a document in your data room repo.

Step 3: catch number formatting bugs explicitly

The article mentions this and it deserves its own validation step, because it's a silent, high-severity bug. Portuguese uses comma as decimal separator and period as thousands separator. English does the reverse. A number like 1.500.000,00 becomes 1,500,000.00, and if that conversion gets fumbled, your ask or valuation can silently change by a factor of a thousand.

def convert_pt_to_en_number(value_str):
    # Portuguese: 1.500.000,50 -> English: 1500000.50
    cleaned = value_str.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
    return float(cleaned)

assert convert_pt_to_en_number("1.500.000,50") == 1500000.50

Run every number that appears in your deck, model, and term sheet through a function like this, then diff the output against what a human translator actually typed into the English version. This catches the single costliest class of error in the entire process.

Step 4: treat your data room as a monorepo with a translation memory

Tools like Weblate, POEditor, or even a translation memory file in the TMX format let you store approved translations of recurring phrases and reuse them automatically across documents. If you're already using an LLM to draft or review translations, feed it the glossary as context rather than letting it improvise terminology per document:

system_prompt = f"""
You are translating investor-facing financial documents from Portuguese to English.
Use only the following approved terminology. Do not substitute synonyms:
{glossary_as_text}
Maintain investor-English register: direct, quantified, no unsupported adjectives.
"""

This won't replace a certified human translator for legal documents like articles of association or board resolutions, where certification and notarisation requirements apply (the source article covers this well, including the Angola-specific case). But for the deck, one-pager, and financial model notes, a glossary-constrained review pass catches most of the drift before it reaches a human reviewer.

Step 5: automate the diff check before every send

Before sending an updated deck to an investor, run a quick script that extracts every number and every glossary term from the new version and diffs it against the previous approved version and the financial model. If MRR changed in the deck but not in the model, or a number's decimal placement looks suspicious, you want that flagged before the investor sees it, not after.

# simple pre-send check
python extract_terms.py deck_v3.md > deck_terms.txt
python extract_terms.py financial_model.md > model_terms.txt
diff deck_terms.txt model_terms.txt

Where this fits with professional translation

None of this replaces a qualified translator for the documents that require certification, or a native-speaker review pass for tone and register, which is where the real skill of adjusting "innovative and disruptive" into something an investor actually trusts lives. What it does is remove the class of error that has nothing to do with translation quality and everything to do with process: inconsistent terms across documents, silent number formatting bugs, and last-minute edits that don't propagate everywhere they should.

If you're raising across borders, build the glossary and the lint step before the round opens, the same way you'd set up CI before a product launch. It's cheap insurance against the kind of mismatch that makes an investor's associate start asking questions you'd rather answer on your own terms.

title: Lesson 10: Run PHP and Nginx with Supervisor in Docker
summary:
Laravel Docker Lessons · Lesson 10

Run Laravel PHP-FPM and Nginx in one optional Docker container with Supervisor, process status checks, foreground logging and graceful shutdown.

This written tutorial follows the actual lesson-10 source snapshot. The published Urdu video lesson is available alongside this written guide.

Continue from Lesson 9, or browse the complete blog.

Earlier lessons use a separate PHP-FPM container and Nginx container. This lesson adds an optional combined container to explain process management: Supervisor starts and monitors both PHP-FPM and Nginx in the foreground. The normal multi-container Compose setup remains available.

Complete file checklist before running commands

Keep docker-compose.yaml as the base service definition and create docker-compose.supervisor.yaml separately. This Supervisor file is standalone on the command line, but its extends entries read web and db from the base file. Do not overwrite the base: a self-reference or missing inherited service will prevent Compose from loading. Create all named configuration files before building. The Dockerfile.supervisor base image must be built from this lesson checkout first.

File Action from the previous lesson Exact source
.docker/nginx/supervisor.conf Create this file; full code included View complete file
.docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf Create this file; full code included View complete file
Dockerfile.supervisor Create this file; full code included View complete file
docker-compose.supervisor.yaml Create this file; full code included View complete file
Dockerfile Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file
docker-compose.yaml Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file

Use the committed lock files from the same tag. They are download/source links rather than abbreviated code samples: composer.lock, package-lock.json.

Create the configuration directories before saving the files:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .docker/supervisor, .docker/nginx

docker-compose.yaml 

x-laravel-environment: &laravel-environment
  DB_URL: ""
  DB_SOCKET: ""
  DB_CONNECTION: mysql
  DB_HOST: db
  DB_PORT: 3306
  DB_DATABASE: laravel_app
  DB_USERNAME: root
  DB_PASSWORD: root
  QUEUE_CONNECTION: database
  DB_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER: 90

x-laravel-service: &laravel-service
  build:
    context: .
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
  image: my-laravel-app
  working_dir: /var/www/html
  user: "www-data"
  volumes:
    - .:/var/www/html
    - /var/www/html/vendor
    - /var/www/html/node_modules
    - /var/www/html/storage
    - /var/www/html/bootstrap/cache
  environment:
    <<: *laravel-environment
    SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "false"
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy

services:
  web:
    <<: *laravel-service

  scheduler:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["scheduler"]
    init: true
    command: ["php", "artisan", "schedule:work", "--no-interaction"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *laravel-environment
      CACHE_STORE: file
      SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "true"

  worker:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["queue"]
    init: true
    command: ["php", "artisan", "queue:work", "database", "--queue=emails", "--sleep=1", "--tries=3", "--timeout=30", "--max-time=3600", "--no-interaction"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 45s

  nginx:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    volumes:
      - .:/var/www/html:ro
      - ./.docker/nginx/default.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - web

  db:
    image: mysql:8.0
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MYSQL_DATABASE: laravel_app
    ports:
      - "${DB_FORWARD_PORT:-3308}:3306"
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/mysql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "mysqladmin ping -h 127.0.0.1 -p\"$${MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD}\" --silent"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 20
      start_period: 20s

volumes:
  dbdata:

docker-compose.supervisor.yaml 

services:
  app:
    extends:
      file: docker-compose.yaml
      service: web
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.supervisor
    image: laravel-supervisor-demo
    user: root
    ports:
      - "${APP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 45s
  db:
    extends:
      file: docker-compose.yaml
      service: db
volumes:
  dbdata:

Check that both files exist with their exact names before running Compose:

Get-Item .\docker-compose.yaml, .\docker-compose.supervisor.yaml

Recording preparation and follow-up checks

Build the base PHP image before the combined Supervisor image. This topology names the Laravel service app, so use exec app. FastCGI targets 127.0.0.1:9000 inside the combined container; the normal separate Nginx service uses web:9000. Stop the previous selected stack before reusing its browser port.

Before recording, follow the recording checklist and PowerShell preflight. Current main excludes generated bootstrap config cache and public/hot from Docker build context. For historical tags, clear old host config cache before rebuilding and renew PHP runtime volumes so earlier database settings are not reused.

Build the combined image

Dockerfile.supervisor builds from the project's my-laravel-app image. Build the base image first so the combined image includes this checkout's PHP extensions, Composer, Node, npm and application dependencies. It installs Debian's Nginx and Supervisor packages, copies the two configuration files and uses Supervisor as its foreground entry command.

docker compose build web
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml build app

The combined container uses root for Supervisor and the Nginx master, allowing Nginx to bind port 80. Nginx workers and PHP-FPM pool workers use www-data. Supervisor's control interface is a local Unix socket; no public management TCP port is added. Do not expose FastCGI port 9000 to the host.

Start the optional topology

Prepare .env and its application key using Lesson 8 first. Stop the previous stack to free port 8080, retaining its volumes. The standalone Supervisor Compose file reuses the existing MySQL service and dbdata named volume when you use the same Compose project name.

docker compose down
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml up -d db app
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec --user www-data app php artisan config:clear
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec --user www-data app php artisan migrate --force
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl status
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app nginx -t

Expect nginx and php-fpm to be RUNNING. Open http://localhost:8080/queue-demo/mail-preview for a Blade page that does not send email. /scheduler-demo also remains available after SQL migrations. APP_PORT can change the host application port.

Understand the two configurations

.docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf enables foreground mode, a local control socket, automatic restart of unexpectedly exited services and logs to Docker stdout/stderr. Rotation is disabled for these special output streams. PHP-FPM runs with -F; Nginx runs with daemon off;. Neither forks into the background and disappears from supervision.

.docker/nginx/supervisor.conf points FastCGI to 127.0.0.1:9000, because both processes share one container. The earlier separate Nginx container uses web:9000; copying that hostname into this combined topology would be incorrect. Both configurations serve Laravel's public directory and pass unmatched requests to index.php.

Supervisor starts PHP-FPM before Nginx. Process priority controls start order, not application readiness; a very early request can still need a retry. The database health check separately gates container startup. Laravel migrations remain an explicit command rather than running every time a process restarts.

Inspect process recovery and logs 

docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl restart php-fpm
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl status
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml logs --tail=40 app

Restarting PHP briefly interrupts requests; use it only in this local teaching demo. Supervisor restarts processes inside the container, while Docker's restart policy handles a stopped container. These are different lifecycles. This example does not also start a queue worker or scheduler inside Supervisor, preventing duplicate background processing.

Stop gracefully 

docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml down

The image uses SIGTERM for Supervisor. It forwards configured shutdown signals to the child process groups; PHP-FPM and Nginx receive QUIT for a graceful exit. The Compose grace period allows time for shutdown. Omit -v to retain the database. For independent scaling, the existing separate-container topology is still available.

How the implementation fits together

Diagram of the implementation in the lesson-10 tag; this is not a production monitoring screenshot.

Configuration and source code

The following files are read directly from this lesson’s Git tag. Later lessons add further capabilities; they do not change this snapshot.

Dockerfile 

FROM php:8.2-fpm

WORKDIR /var/www/html

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    libzip-dev \
    libpq-dev \
    unzip \
    && docker-php-ext-install zip pdo_mysql pdo_pgsql pcntl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN pecl install mongodb-1.21.2 \
    && docker-php-ext-enable mongodb

COPY --from=composer:2 /usr/bin/composer /usr/local/bin/composer
ENV COMPOSER_HOME=/tmp/composer

COPY --from=node:22-bookworm-slim /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
COPY --from=node:22-bookworm-slim /usr/local/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules
RUN ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npm \
    && ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npx-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npx \
    && node --version && npm --version
ENV NPM_CONFIG_CACHE=/tmp/npm-cache

COPY --chown=www-data:www-data . /var/www/html

RUN COMPOSER_ALLOW_SUPERUSER=1 composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader \
    && mkdir -p node_modules \
    && chown -R www-data:www-data vendor storage bootstrap/cache node_modules /tmp/composer \
    && chmod -R 775 storage bootstrap/cache

Dockerfile.supervisor 

FROM my-laravel-app:latest

USER root

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends nginx supervisor \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default

COPY .docker/nginx/supervisor.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/laravel.conf
COPY .docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf /etc/supervisor/supervisord.conf

EXPOSE 80
STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM
CMD ["/usr/bin/supervisord", "-c", "/etc/supervisor/supervisord.conf"]

.docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf 

[unix_http_server]
file=/tmp/supervisor.sock
chmod=0700

[supervisord]
nodaemon=true
user=root
pidfile=/tmp/supervisord.pid
logfile=/dev/stdout
logfile_maxbytes=0

[rpcinterface:supervisor]
supervisor.rpcinterface_factory=supervisor.rpcinterface:make_main_rpcinterface

[supervisorctl]
serverurl=unix:///tmp/supervisor.sock

[program:php-fpm]
command=/usr/local/sbin/php-fpm -F
priority=10
autostart=true
autorestart=true
startsecs=3
stopsignal=QUIT
stopwaitsecs=20
stopasgroup=true
killasgroup=true
stdout_logfile=/dev/stdout
stdout_logfile_maxbytes=0
stderr_logfile=/dev/stderr
stderr_logfile_maxbytes=0

[program:nginx]
command=/usr/sbin/nginx -g "daemon off;"
priority=20

Laravel Docker Lessons · Lesson 10

Run Laravel PHP-FPM and Nginx in one optional Docker container with Supervisor, process status checks, foreground logging and graceful shutdown.

This written tutorial follows the actual lesson-10 source snapshot. The published Urdu video lesson is available alongside this written guide.

Continue from Lesson 9, or browse the complete blog.

Earlier lessons use a separate PHP-FPM container and Nginx container. This lesson adds an optional combined container to explain process management: Supervisor starts and monitors both PHP-FPM and Nginx in the foreground. The normal multi-container Compose setup remains available.

Complete file checklist before running commands

Keep docker-compose.yaml as the base service definition and create docker-compose.supervisor.yaml separately. This Supervisor file is standalone on the command line, but its extends entries read web and db from the base file. Do not overwrite the base: a self-reference or missing inherited service will prevent Compose from loading. Create all named configuration files before building. The Dockerfile.supervisor base image must be built from this lesson checkout first.

.docker/nginx/supervisor.conf Create this file; full code included View complete file
.docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf Create this file; full code included View complete file

Dockerfile Keep the inherited file; inspect the exact snapshot View complete file

Use the committed lock files from the same tag. They are download/source links rather than abbreviated code samples: composer.lock, package-lock.json.

Create the configuration directories before saving the files:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .docker/supervisor, .docker/nginx

docker-compose.yaml

  DB_SOCKET: ""

  DB_HOST: db
  DB_PORT: 3306

  DB_USERNAME: root
  DB_PASSWORD: root
  QUEUE_CONNECTION: database
  DB_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER: 90

x-laravel-service: &laravel-service
  build:
    context: .
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
  image: my-laravel-app
  working_dir: /var/www/html
  user: "www-data"
  volumes:
    - .:/var/www/html
    - /var/www/html/vendor
    - /var/www/html/node_modules
    - /var/www/html/storage
    - /var/www/html/bootstrap/cache
  environment:
    <<: *laravel-environment
    SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "false"

    db:

services:
  web:
    <<: *laravel-service

  scheduler:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["scheduler"]
    init: true

    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      <<: *laravel-environment
      CACHE_STORE: file
      SCHEDULER_DEMO_ENABLED: "true"

  worker:
    <<: *laravel-service
    profiles: ["queue"]
    init: true

Get-Item .\docker-compose.yaml, .\docker-compose.supervisor.yaml

Recording preparation and follow-up checks

Build the base PHP image before the combined Supervisor image. This topology names the Laravel service app, so use exec app. FastCGI targets 127.0.0.1:9000 inside the combined container; the normal separate Nginx service uses web:9000. Stop the previous selected stack before reusing its browser port.

Before recording, follow the recording checklist and PowerShell preflight. Current main excludes generated bootstrap config cache and public/hot from Docker build context. For historical tags, clear old host config cache before rebuilding and renew PHP runtime volumes so earlier database settings are not reused.

Build the combined image

Dockerfile.supervisor builds from the project's my-laravel-app image. Build the base image first so the combined image includes this checkout's PHP extensions, Composer, Node, npm and application dependencies. It installs Debian's Nginx and Supervisor packages, copies the two configuration files and uses Supervisor as its foreground entry command.

docker compose build web
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml build app

The combined container uses root for Supervisor and the Nginx master, allowing Nginx to bind port 80. Nginx workers and PHP-FPM pool workers use www-data. Supervisor's control interface is a local Unix socket; no public management TCP port is added. Do not expose FastCGI port 9000 to the host.

Start the optional topology

Prepare .env and its application key using Lesson 8 first. Stop the previous stack to free port 8080, retaining its volumes. The standalone Supervisor Compose file reuses the existing MySQL service and dbdata named volume when you use the same Compose project name.

docker compose down
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml up -d db app
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec --user www-data app php artisan config:clear
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec --user www-data app php artisan migrate --force
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl status
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app nginx -t

Expect nginx and php-fpm to be RUNNING. Open http://localhost:8080/queue-demo/mail-preview for a Blade page that does not send email. /scheduler-demo also remains available after SQL migrations. APP_PORT can change the host application port.

Understand the two configurations

.docker/supervisor/supervisord.conf enables foreground mode, a local control socket, automatic restart of unexpectedly exited services and logs to Docker stdout/stderr. Rotation is disabled for these special output streams. PHP-FPM runs with -F; Nginx runs with daemon off;. Neither forks into the background and disappears from supervision.

.docker/nginx/supervisor.conf points FastCGI to 127.0.0.1:9000, because both processes share one container. The earlier separate Nginx container uses web:9000; copying that hostname into this combined topology would be incorrect. Both configurations serve Laravel's public directory and pass unmatched requests to index.php.

Supervisor starts PHP-FPM before Nginx. Process priority controls start order, not application readiness; a very early request can still need a retry. The database health check separately gates container startup. Laravel migrations remain an explicit command rather than running every time a process restarts.

Inspect process recovery and logs 

docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl restart php-fpm
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml exec app supervisorctl status
docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml logs --tail=40 app

Restarting PHP briefly interrupts requests; use it only in this local teaching demo. Supervisor restarts processes inside the container, while Docker's restart policy handles a stopped container. These are different lifecycles. This example does not also start a queue worker or scheduler inside Supervisor, preventing duplicate background processing.

Stop gracefully 

docker compose -f docker-compose.supervisor.yaml down

The image uses SIGTERM for Supervisor. It forwards configured shutdown signals to the child process groups; PHP-FPM and Nginx receive QUIT for a graceful exit. The Compose grace period allows time for shutdown. Omit -v to retain the database. For independent scaling, the existing separate-container topology is still available.

How the implementation fits together

Diagram of the implementation in the lesson-10 tag; this is not a production monitoring screenshot.

Dockerfile 

FROM php:8.2-fpm

WORKDIR /var/www/html

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    libzip-dev \
    libpq-dev \
    unzip \
    && docker-php-ext-install zip pdo_mysql pdo_pgsql pcntl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN pecl install mongodb-1.21.2 \
    && docker-php-ext-enable mongodb

    && chown -R www-data:www-data vendor storage bootstrap/cache node_modules /tmp/composer \
